chapters.desc: Forty-one abyāt on the karāmāt of the awliyāʾ, the righteous friends of Allah, as Ahl al-Sunnah believe in them: who the awliyāʾ are, the kinds of extraordinary occurrence and how a karāmah differs from a prophet’s miracle and from what is satanic, examples from the Qurʾān and the Sunnah, and the greatest karāmah of all: worshipping Allah with steadfastness.

verses.tr: Thus speaks Waleed ibn Idrīs, hoping for Your forgiveness: My Lord, to You alone I turn, and from You alone I seek refuge.

exp.en:
Translator’s foreword

In the Name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful

All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds. May His peace and blessings be upon our master Muḥammad ﷺ, his family, his Companions, and all who follow his guidance until the Final Day.

Among the many treasures preserved within the Arabic language are concise works that distil profound Islamic beliefs into elegant poetry. Such works have traditionally been memorised, studied and transmitted from teacher to student across generations. Unfortunately, many Muslims who do not read Arabic remain unable to benefit directly from these remarkable texts.

It is this reality that inspired the present translation.

I was honoured to receive an ijāzah from the author of this work, Shaykh Dr Waleed ibn Idrīs al-Menesee (حفظه الله), permitting me to translate this poem and all his authored works. Receiving this authorisation was not merely an academic milestone, but a responsibility to help convey beneficial knowledge to those who sincerely seek it.

This translation therefore is not intended to replace the original Arabic. Rather, it is an invitation to it. Alongside the translation, I have included explanatory notes, diagrams, visual summaries and clarifications to assist students, teachers and general readers in understanding the beautiful principles contained within this work.

The subject of this poem is the karāmāt (miraculous honours) granted to the Awliyāʾ (the righteous friends of Allah) according to the creed of Ahl al-Sunnah wa’l-Jamā‘ah. In an age filled with sensationalism and exaggerated claims, this subject deserves to be studied with balance, evidence and scholarly precision.

Yet as I repeatedly returned to this poem, one verse continued to resonate above all the others:

واعلم بأن أكرم الكرامة… أن تعبد الله على استقامة

“Know that the greatest miracle is that you worship Allah with steadfastness.”

This single line captures the essence of the entire work.

The greatest honour bestowed upon the righteous was never walking upon water, travelling extraordinary distances, or witnessing remarkable events. Those were exceptional occurrences granted by Allah to whomever He willed.

Their greatest miracle was something far greater.

It was unwavering faith.

It was sincerity hidden from people.

It was consistency in worship.

It was remaining steadfast upon the Qurʾān and Sunnah until their final breath.

True greatness is not found in extraordinary moments; it is found in extraordinary consistency.

May Allah grant us beneficial knowledge, sincere actions, sound belief, and above all, steadfastness until we meet Him.

Abdullah Badat

The Basmalah

The author begins with the Basmalah, following the example of the Book of Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, for Allah Himself opened His Book with the Basmalah. He also follows the example of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in his correspondence, as he would begin the letters he sent to kings with the Basmalah, such as his letter to Heraclius: “In the Name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. From Muḥammad, the Messenger of Allah, to Heraclius, the ruler of the Romans.”

Likewise, the Prophet of Allah, Sulaymān (peace be upon him), began the letter he wrote to Bilqīs and the people of Yemen with the Basmalah, as Allah says:

“Indeed, it is from Sulaymān, and indeed it reads: ‘In the Name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.’” (Sūrah al-Naml 27:30)

Since this poem is a written composition, it may be treated according to the rulings pertaining to written works. It is therefore from the Sunnah to begin books and written works with the Basmalah, while sermons are begun with the praise of Allah, Glorified and Exalted.

There are also narrations whose chains contain some weakness. However, they fall under the category of narrations concerning virtuous deeds (Faḍāʾil al-Aʿmāl), in which weak narrations may be acted upon according to the well-known conditions. Among them is the narration: “Every matter that is not begun with ‘Bismillāh’ is cut off (from blessing),” or, according to another wording, “is deficient.” Furthermore, its meaning is supported by numerous texts that establish the beginning of many righteous deeds with the Basmalah.

وإليك ألتجي

Seeking refuge in Allah means asking Him to remove harm and grant protection.

The author introduces himself as one who hopes for his Lord’s forgiveness and turns to Him alone for refuge. Seeking refuge in Allah means asking Him to remove harm and grant protection.

Translator’s reflection

Every journey of sacred knowledge should begin with humility. Before seeking to understand the miracles granted to Allah’s friends, Shaykh Waleed reminds us that every seeker is first and foremost a servant in need of Allah’s forgiveness and protection.

verses.tr: I believe in Allah, Who, in His wisdom, chose from among mankind His Messengers, honouring them above all creation.

exp.en:
اصطفى

Means that Allah selected and chose His Messengers, granting them distinction over His servants.

رُسْلَهُ

The author pronounces the sīn with sukūn (رُسْلَهُ) for the sake of poetic metre. This is an established linguistic usage found in some Qurʾānic readings.

فُعُل

Linguistically, the middle letter (ʿayn al-kalimah) of a plural noun on this pattern may be rendered sākin. Examples include سُبُل becomin سُبْل and كُتُب becoming كُتْب.

The poet then affirms that Allah has chosen His Messengers, selecting them and granting them distinction over His servants.

Translator’s reflection

Before we learn about the Awliyāʾ, we must understand the Prophets. Islam never allows admiration of the righteous to eclipse the status of Allah’s Messengers. The Awliyāʾ are honoured because they follow the Prophets, not because they possess extraordinary abilities.

Living this bayt

Our age often celebrates personalities, charisma, and extraordinary stories. This bayt reminds us that true honour is measured by closeness to revelation. If Allah Himself chose the Messengers as the greatest of creation, then our own honour lies in following them. The closer we are to the Sunnah, the closer we are to the path of Allah’s friends.

ajuzW.g: and follows in the footsteps of

verses.tr: And I believe in the miracles granted to Allah’s righteous friends, those who obey His command and faithfully follow the Prophetic way.

exp.en:
وَهْوَ

The author pronounces the hāʾ with sukūn (وَهْوَ), in accordance with the narration of Qālūn and those who concur with him.

اقْتَفَى Means to follow or follow in someone’s footsteps.

The poet explains that he believes in everything that has come from Allah, as well as everything that Allah and His Messenger ﷺ have informed us of.

Among the matters that we believe in is the karāmāt (miraculous honours) of the awliyāʾ (the righteous friends of Allah), as Imām al-Ṭaḥāwī رحمه الله said: “We do not give preference to any of the awliyāʾ over any of the Prophets عليهم السلام. Rather, we say that a single Prophet is superior to all of the awliyāʾ combined. We believe in the karāmāt of the awliyāʾ and in the authentic reports transmitted from trustworthy narrators concerning them.”

Accordingly, we affirm the karāmāt of the awliyāʾ and believe that Allah honours whomever He wills from among His righteous servants with whatever forms of karāmah He wills.

Definition of Awliyāʾ

The walī obeys the command of Allah and follows the Sunnah; that is, he adheres to it and acts in accordance with it.

The awliyāʾ of Allah, therefore, are those who fulfil the obligatory duties and draw nearer to Allah, the Highest, through voluntary acts of worship.

The awliyāʾ fall into two categories:

  • Those who draw near to Allah by fulfilling the obligatory acts.
  • Those who go beyond that by drawing nearer to Him through both the obligatory and the voluntary acts of worship.

The proof for this is the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah رضي الله عنه recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ narrated that Allah, the Exalted, said:

“Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I declare war upon him. My servant draws no nearer to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him. Then My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts until I love him. When I love him, I become his hearing by which he hears, his sight by which he sees, his hand by which he grasps, and his foot by which he walks. If he asks of Me, I shall surely give him, and if he seeks My protection, I shall surely grant him protection. Never do I hesitate concerning anything I do as I hesitate concerning the soul of the believing servant: he dislikes death, and I dislike causing him distress.”

This ḥadīth contains a warning against showing enmity towards the awliyāʾ of Allah. By implication, it commands us to love them, not to harbour hatred towards them, nor to oppose them. Allah has informed those who oppose His awliyāʾ that He Himself will wage war against them.

The ḥadīth first mentions drawing near to Allah through the obligatory acts of worship and then mentions drawing near to Him through the voluntary acts.

Thus, the walī is the one who seeks nearness to Allah by means of both the obligatory and the voluntary acts of worship.

The ḥadīth also indicates that Allah protects His awliyāʾ in the use of their faculties and senses, safeguarding them from disobedience. This is the meaning of His statement: “When I love him, I become his hearing by which he hears, his sight by which he sees, his hand by which he grasps, and his foot by which he walks.”

It also indicates that Allah answers the supplications of His righteous servants.

Translator’s reflection

In an age fascinated by the extraordinary, this bayt redirects our attention to the ordinary acts performed with extraordinary consistency. A person may never witness a miracle, yet if he obeys Allah and follows the Sunnah, he has attained the qualities of a walī. Conversely, a person may amaze people with unusual occurrences, but if he neglects Allah’s commands or abandons the Sunnah, those occurrences are not evidence of sainthood.

Living this bayt

Every Muslim can ask two simple questions: 1. Am I obeying Allah’s commands? 2. Am I striving to walk in the footsteps of His Messenger ﷺ? If the answer is yes, then one is walking the path of the Awliyāʾ.

The goal is not to seek karāmāt. The goal is to seek istiqāmah. And when Allah grants someone extraordinary honours, they are merely the fruit of a life rooted in obedience and devotion.

verses.tr: The Qurʾān declares that Allah’s friends are those who believe, then live with God-consciousness; they are given glad tidings that they shall have no fear.

exp.en:
الْقُرْآنِ

The author writes (القرآن) with the hamzah omitted and its vowel transferred to the rāʾ, in accordance with the reading of Ibn Kathīr, for the sake of maintaining the poetic metre.

آمَنُوا وَيَأْمَنُوا

The author uses two expressions derived from the same Arabic root (أ م ن). The first, آمَنُوا, means that they believed, while the second, يَأْمَنُوا, means that they attain security. This creates a beautiful connection between their faith and the security promised to them by Allah.

The poet explains that Allah defines His Awliyā’ in the Qur’an as those who possess two essential qualities:

  • Īmān (faith)
  • Taqwā (consciousness of Allah).

Allah says:

﴿أَلَآ إِنَّ أَوۡلِيَآءَ ٱللَّهِ لَا خَوۡفٌ عَلَيۡهِمۡ وَلَا هُمۡ يَحۡزَنُونَ ٦٢ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَكَانُواْ يَتَّقُونَ٦٣ لَهُمُ ٱلۡبُشۡرَىٰ فِي ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَا وَفِي ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِۚ لَا تَبۡدِيلَ لِكَلِمَٰتِ ٱللَّهِۚ ذَٰلِكَ هُوَ ٱلۡفَوۡزُ ٱلۡعَظِيمُ٦٤﴾

“Indeed, the friends of Allah will have no fear, nor will they grieve. Those who believed and were conscious of Allah. For them are glad tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter. There is no changing the words of Allah. That is the supreme success.” Sūrah Yūnus 10:62–64

Allah therefore identifies His Awliyā’ through their faith and taqwā and promises them glad tidings and security.

1. The Promise of Security

Allah promises His Awliyā’ that they will have no fear and will not grieve. This is because they feared Allah during their worldly lives, and Allah will grant them security in the Hereafter.

Abū Hurayrah رضي الله عنه narrates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah declares:

“By My Might, I shall not combine two fears for My servant, nor shall I combine two states of security for him. If he feels secure from Me in the world, I shall make him fear on the Day of Resurrection; and if he fears Me in the world, I shall grant him security on the Day of Resurrection.” Ibn Ḥibbān

2. The Glad Tidings of the Awliyā’

Allah says:

﴿لَهُمُ ٱلۡبُشۡرَىٰ فِي ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَا وَفِي ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِۚ ﴾

“For them are glad tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter.” Sūrah Yūnus 10:64

The meaning of these glad tidings is explained in several narrations. Abū al-Dardāʾ رضي الله عنه was asked about this verse. He explained that he had asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it, and the Prophet ﷺ replied: “No one has asked me about this besides you since it was revealed. It refers to the righteous dream that a Muslim sees or that is seen for him.” al-Ḥākim

Abū Hurayrah رضي الله عنه also narrates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Nothing remains of Prophethood except the glad tidings.” They asked, “What are the glad tidings?” He replied: “The righteous dream.” al-Bukhārī

Another narration from Ibn ʿAbbās رضي الله عنهما mentions that the Prophet ﷺ announced that nothing remains of the glad tidings of Prophethood except the righteous dream that a Muslim sees or that is seen for him. al-Bukhārī

The Prophet ﷺ also explained that when people praise a believer for a good deed he has performed, this is an immediate glad tiding for the believer.

3. The Forms of Glad Tidings

The author explains that the glad tidings granted to Allah’s Awliyā’ in this world take several forms:

1. Allah’s support and assistance: Allah informs His righteous servants that He is with them through His support and assistance.

﴿إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ مَعَ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّقَواْ وَّٱلَّذِينَ هُم مُّحۡسِنُونَ١٢٨﴾

Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good. Sūrah al-Naḥl 16:128

Allah also says:

﴿إِنَّا لَنَنصُرُ رُسُلَنَا وَٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ فِي ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَا وَيَوۡمَ يَقُومُ ٱلۡأَشۡهَٰدُ٥١﴾

Indeed, We will support Our Messengers and those who believe during the life of this world and on the Day when the witnesses will stand. Sūrah Ghāfir 40:51

2. Glad tidings of the Hereafter: Allah informs His righteous servants of the blessings and pleasure He has prepared for them.

﴿وَبَشِّرِ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَعَمِلُواْ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ أَنَّ لَهُمۡ جَنَّٰتٖ تَجۡرِي مِن تَحۡتِهَا ٱلۡأَنۡهَٰرُۖ ...الآية٢٥﴾

Give glad tidings to those who believe and perform righteous deeds that they will have gardens beneath which rivers flow. Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:25

3. Allah’s care and protection: Allah grants His walī success and protects his faculties from disobedience, as mentioned in the ḥadīth of Allah’s love for His servant:

“I become his hearing by which he hears, his sight by which he sees...” Muslim

4. The glad tidings of the angels at death: When the soul is about to depart, the angels give the righteous glad tidings of Paradise.

﴿إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ قَالُواْ رَبُّنَا ٱللَّهُ ثُمَّ ٱسۡتَقَٰمُواْ تَتَنَزَّلُ عَلَيۡهِمُ ٱلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ أَلَّا تَخَافُواْ وَلَا تَحۡزَنُواْ وَأَبۡشِرُواْ بِٱلۡجَنَّةِ ٱلَّتِي كُنتُمۡ تُوعَدُونَ٣٠﴾

Indeed, those who say, “Our Lord is Allah,” and then remain steadfast, the angels descend upon them, saying: “Do not fear, nor grieve, but receive the glad tidings of Paradise which you were promised.” Sūrah Fuṣṣilat 41:30

These glad tidings continue through the stages of the Hereafter: the blessings of the grave, drinking from the Ḥawḍ, receiving one’s book of deeds in the right hand, the weighing of deeds, ease in crossing the Ṣirāṭ, and eventually entering Paradise.

5. Righteous dreams: A believer may see something good in his sleep, or something good may be shown to others concerning him. This is among the glad tidings mentioned in the narrations above.

6. The acceptance of supplication: Allah may grant His walī the blessing of having his supplications answered. This is indicated in the previously discussed ḥadīth: “If he asks Me, I shall surely give him.”

7. Extraordinary occurrences: Allah may cause remarkable events, beyond ordinary human ability, to take place through the hands of His walī.

Examples include the events involving Maryam عليها السلام, the People of the Cave, the boy and the sorcerer, and the infant who spoke to his mother in the story of the Trench.

However, the occurrence of such extraordinary events is not a condition for being a walī. They may occur, or they may not.

Translator’s reflection

There is something profoundly comforting about Allah’s definition of a walī. He does not describe them as scholars, ascetics, or people known by the masses. He describes them with two qualities that every believer can strive for: Faith and Taqwā.

This means that the door of wilāyah is open to every sincere Muslim. Nearness to Allah is not reserved for a spiritual elite—it is the destination of anyone who believes sincerely and lives with conscious obedience to Him.

Living this bayt

When many people hear the word walī, they think of someone extraordinary. The Qurʾān invites us to think differently. A walī is not first recognised by what people see, but by what Allah sees: a heart firm in faith and a life adorned with taqwā.

The promise of Allah is therefore not reserved for the famous or the remarkable. It belongs to every believer who strives to draw near to Him through faith, obedience, and perseverance.

verses.tr: When the friend of my Lord is seen, my Lord is remembered because of him, and this is well known in the Hadith.

exp.en:
The poet explains that whenever one sees a walī (the friend of Allah), one remembers Allah through him. This meaning is found in a well-known ḥadīth narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās رضي الله عنهما, in which the Prophet ﷺ was asked: “Who are the awliyāʾ of Allah?”

He replied: “Those who, when they are seen, Allah is remembered.” al-Ḍiyāʾ al-Maqdisī in al-Aḥādīth al-Mukhtārah, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Kabīr and al-Nasāʾī in al-Kubrā

Among the distinguishing qualities of the awliyāʾ is that their very presence reminds people of Allah, Glorified and Exalted. This includes being reminded of His worship, obedience to Him, righteous deeds, beneficial knowledge, and everything that draws a person nearer to Allah.

Translator’s reflection

The truest measure of our relationship with Allah is not how often we speak about Him, but how naturally people remember Him after spending time with us. A heart filled with Allah cannot help but leave His traces wherever it goes.

Living this bayt

Not everyone is destined to become famous. Not everyone will deliver lectures or write books. But every believer can strive to become someone whose honesty, humility, mercy, and devotion quietly remind others of Allah.

Sometimes the most powerful daʿwah is not delivered from a pulpit; it is lived in daily interactions.

verses.tr: The friends of Allah are of two ranks: those who tread the balanced path, and those noble souls who race ahead in righteousness.

exp.en:
الْكُرَمَا

The poet intends الْكُرَمَاءُ, meaning “ the noble ones” or “the honourable ones.” The hamzah is omitted to maintain the poetic metre.

The author explains that the Awliyā’ of Allah fall into two categories:

  • Al-Muqtaṣidūn (those who are moderate)
  • Al-Sābiqūn (those who are foremost in good deeds).

To explain these categories, the author refers to the Ayah in which Allah divides those who inherit His Book into three groups.

Allah says:

﴿ثُمَّ أَوۡرَثۡنَا ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱصۡطَفَيۡنَا مِنۡ عِبَادِنَاۖ فَمِنۡهُمۡ ظَالِمٞ لِّنَفۡسِهِۦ وَمِنۡهُم مُّقۡتَصِدٞ وَمِنۡهُمۡ سَابِقُۢ بِٱلۡخَيۡرَٰتِ بِإِذۡنِ ٱللَّهِۚ ذَٰلِكَ هُوَ ٱلۡفَضۡلُ ٱلۡكَبِيرُ٣٢﴾

“Then We caused the Book to be inherited by those We chose from among Our servants. Among them are those who wrong themselves, those who are moderate, and those who are foremost in good deeds by Allah’s permission. That is the great bounty.” Sūrah Fāṭir 35:32

The Ayah identifies three categories among those whom Allah chose to inherit His Book:

1. Those Who Wrong Themselves (الظَّالِمُونَ لِأَنْفُسِهِمْ)

These are those who fall into certain sins or neglect some of the obligatory duties.

2. The Moderate Ones (الْمُقْتَصِدُونَ)

These are those who fulfil the obligatory duties and abstain from prohibited actions, limiting themselves to these obligations without going beyond them.

3. Those Foremost in Good Deeds (السَّابِقُونَ بِالْخَيْرَاتِ)

These are those who draw nearer to Allah through voluntary acts of worship and go beyond the obligatory duties by also abstaining from disliked actions and doubtful matters.

The Two Categories of Awliyā’

The author further explains that Allah refers to those who are foremost in good deeds as al-Muqarrabūn (those brought near to Allah) in other passages of the Qur’an.

Allah says:

﴿وَٱلسَّٰبِقُونَ ٱلسَّٰبِقُونَ١٠ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ ٱلۡمُقَرَّبُونَ ١١﴾

“And the foremost are the foremost. Those are the ones brought near to Allah.” Sūrah al-Wāqiʿah 56:10–11

As for the moderate ones, Allah refers to them in certain sūrahs as الأبرار (the righteous) and in others as أصحاب اليمين (the companions of the right). Thus, المقتصدون, الأبرار and أصحاب اليمين refer to one category of believers.

Accordingly, the Awliyā’ of Allah are of two categories:

1. Al-Muqtaṣid (المُقْتَصِد)

The one who limits himself to fulfilling the obligatory duties and abstaining from prohibited actions, without going beyond that.

2. Al-Sābiq (السَّابِق)

The one who draws nearer to Allah through voluntary acts of worship, while also abstaining from disliked actions and doubtful matters.

Thus, the author establishes that the Awliyā’ are not distinguished by extraordinary occurrences, but by their faith, obedience, and devotion to Allah.

Translator’s reflection

This bayt reminds us that the journey to Allah is not a competition against His servants; it is a lifelong pursuit of His pleasure.

Some walk with measured steps, faithfully preserving their obligations. Others hasten forward, filling their lives with voluntary acts of worship, service, and remembrance. Both are honoured, yet the Qurʾān gently encourages us never to become complacent. Every sunrise is an invitation to take one step closer to Allah than we were yesterday.

Living this bayt

Every believer should strive to move from consistency to excellence.

Steadfastness is beautiful, but love inspires eagerness. The believer who loves Allah does not ask: “What is the minimum required?” He asks: “What more can I do to draw nearer to my Lord?”

verses.tr: No friend of Allah persists in wronging himself or others. Know this well and hold firmly to it.

exp.en:
The author explains that a person who is ظَالِمٌ لِنَفْسِهِ, wronging himself through sins and disobedience, is not included among the Awliyāʾ while he remains in that state. The same applies to one who is ظَالِمٌ لِغَيْرِهِ, wronging others through transgression.

This understanding was mentioned by Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah: and other leading scholars. They explain that the Awliyāʾ of Allah include the two categories mentioned previously: السَّابِقُونَ (those foremost in good deeds) and الْمُقْتَصِدُونَ(those who are moderate). The ظَالِمُ لِنَفْسِهِ, however, is not included among them.

Two Types of ظلم

The author then explains that ظلم is of two types:

1. Shirk (الشِّرْك)

The first type of ظلم is shirk. This is established by the explanation given by the Prophet ﷺ when the Companions found the following verse difficult to understand:

﴿الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَلَمْ يَلْبِسُوا إِيمَانَهُم بِظُلْمٍ أُولَٰئِكَ لَهُمُ الْأَمْنُ وَهُم مُّهْتَدُونَ﴾

“Those who believe and do not mix their faith with injustice, they will have security, and they are rightly guided.” Al-Anʿām 6:82

ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd رضي الله عنه narrated that when this Ayah was revealed, the Muslims found it difficult and asked: يَا رَسُولَ اللهِ، أَيُّنَا لَا يَظْلِمُ نَفْسَهُ؟ “O Messenger of Allah, which one of us does not wrong himself?”

The Prophet ﷺ replied:

لَيْسَ ذَلِكَ، إِنَّمَا هُوَ الشِّرْكُ، أَلَمْ تَسْمَعُوا مَا قَالَ لُقْمَانُ لِابْنِهِ وَهُوَ يَعِظُهُ: ﴿يَا بُنَيَّ لَا تُشْرِكْ بِاللَّهِ ۖ إِنَّ الشِّرْكَ لَظُلْمٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾

“That is not what is meant. Rather, it is shirk. Have you not heard what Luqmān said to his son while advising him?” “O my son, do not associate anything with Allah. Indeed, associating others with Allah is a tremendous injustice.” Luqmān 31:13

The Prophet ﷺ thus clarified that the ظلم referred to in this verse is الشِّرْك, associating partners with Allah.

2. Sins and Disobedience (الذُّنُوبُ وَالْمَعَاصِي)

The second type of ظلم is committing sins and acts of disobedience. This is the meaning intended in the Ayah:

﴿فَمِنْهُمْ ظَالِمٌ لِنَفْسِهِ﴾

“Among them are those who wrong themselves.” Fāṭir 35:32

The author explains that this Ayah refers to the Muslims, among whom are those who wrong themselves through sins and disobedience. Such wrongdoing may even become so severe that it reaches the level of shirk, and we seek Allah’s protection from that.

Allah also describes those who have not repented as ظَالِمُونَ:

﴿وَمَن لَمْ يَتُبْ فَأُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الظَّالِمُونَ﴾

“And whoever does not repent, then those are the wrongdoers.” Al-Ḥujurāt 49:11

Thus, whoever has not repented from his sins falls under the category of one who wrongs himself. A person may also wrong others through insults, verbal abuse, unlawfully taking their wealth, striking them, killing them, and other forms of transgression.

The Criterion is One’s Final End

The author then highlights an important principle:

وَالْعِبْرَةُ بِالْخَوَاتِيمِ - What matters is how a person’s life comes to an end.

Every believer may fall into some form of sin or disobedience. However, what matters is the state in which a person ultimately ends his life. If he sins, then repents to Allah and returns to Him, he regains the quality through which he deserves to be counted among the Awliyāʾ of Allah.

Therefore, while a person is engaged in wrongdoing, he is not counted among the Awliyāʾ in that state. However, if his life concludes with repentance and steadfastness, and he becomes among أَصْحَابِ الْيَمِينِ or الْمُقَرَّبِينَ, then he is among the Awliyāʾ of Allah.

The author supports this with the statement of the Prophet ﷺ:

كُلُّ ابْنِ آدَمَ خَطَّاءٌ، وَخَيْرُ الْخَطَّائِينَ التَّوَّابُونَ.

“Every son of Ādam commits mistakes, and the best of those who commit mistakes are those who constantly repent.” al-Tirmidhī

Translator’s reflection

One of the greatest dangers in every age is confusing charisma with righteousness. A person may attract crowds, tell remarkable stories, or even be surrounded by extraordinary claims. Yet the Qurʾān teaches us to look elsewhere. Look at how they worship. Look at how they treat their family, their neighbours, and those under their care. Look at whether they uphold the rights of Allah and the rights of His servants.

Living this bayt

Before admiring someone’s extraordinary qualities, ask a simpler question:

Do they fulfil Allah’s rights?

Do they honour the rights of His creation?

The greatest miracle is not an unusual event. It is a heart that refuses to wrong Allah through disobedience and refuses to wrong people through oppression.

verses.tr: A karāmah is an extraordinary occurrence that goes beyond the customary order of things, taking place through a righteous servant who is not a Prophet.

exp.en:
The author now defines الكرامة (a karāmah), explaining that it is the appearance of something extraordinary through a servant who is outwardly righteous and is not a Prophet, either at the time the occurrence takes place or afterwards.

He gives this as the most precise definition, although karāmah has also been defined in other ways.

The Condition of Outward Righteousness

The phrase “through the hands of an outwardly righteous servant” is an important qualification in the definition.

It excludes the extraordinary occurrences that may appear through the hands of the wicked, disbelievers, and those who are astray or engaged in religious innovation. Examples include magicians, soothsayers, the False Messiah (المَسِيحُ الدَّجَّالُ), and others of the misguided.

If something extraordinary occurs through such people, it is not regarded as a karāmah. Rather, it may be a satanic occurrence or an act of magic.

The author further explains that the servant through whom a karāmah occurs must not be a Prophet either in the present (الحال) or in the future (المآل).

In other words, he must not be a Prophet when the extraordinary occurrence takes place, nor may he become a Prophet afterwards.

The author gives the example of our Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ. He was not yet a Prophet before reaching the age of forty, as Allah granted him Prophethood at that age. Likewise, most of the Prophets were granted Prophethood at the age of forty.

Therefore, any extraordinary occurrence that takes place through a Prophet before he receives Prophethood is given a particular name by the scholars: الإِرْهَاصُ (Irhāṣ).

Translator’s reflection

The world is often captivated by what is unusual. Islam, however, redirects our gaze. It teaches us to marvel not first at extraordinary events, but at extraordinary people; ordinary servants whose hearts have become so devoted to Allah that, if He wills, He may honour them with something beyond the ordinary. The true wonder is never the karāmah itself. The true wonder is the life of faith, humility, and unwavering istiqāmah that preceded it.

Living this bayt

Our fascination should never be with the extraordinary event itself.

Instead, we should ask: What kind of person did Allah choose to honour with such an event?

The answer is always the same: A servant distinguished not by spectacle, but by sincerity, obedience, humility, and steadfastness.

That is the real miracle.

verses.tr: Extraordinary occurrences are of various kinds: the Karāmah, the Muʿjizah, the Irhāṣ, and Divine Assistance (Maʿūnah).

exp.en:
Abyāt 9–10

كَرَامَةٌ

An extraordinary occurrence granted by Allah through a righteous servant who is not a Prophet.

مُعْجِزَةٌ

An extraordinary occurrence granted by Allah through a Prophet, accompanied by a claim to Prophethood.

إِرْهَاصٌ

An extraordinary occurrence granted by Allah through a future Prophet before his Prophethood.

مَعُونَةٌ

An extraordinary occurrence through which Allah assists an ordinary or weak Muslim, delivering him from hardship and difficulty.

الِاسْتِدْرَاجُ

An extraordinary occurrence granted to a sinful person in accordance with what he desires, gradually leading him further into misguidance.

السِّحْرُ

An extraordinary occurrence performed through a sinful person, allowing him to continue further in his misguidance.

The author now explains that خَوَارِقُ الْعَادَةِ (extraordinary occurrences that go beyond the customary order of things) are divided into eight categories. Each has a different nature and occurs under different circumstances.

1. كَرَامَةُ الْوَلِيّ – The Karāmah of a Walī

A karāmah is an extraordinary occurrence that Allah brings about through the hands of an outwardly righteous servant, who follows the Prophet whose Sharīʿah he is required to follow, possesses sound belief, and performs righteous deeds. This may occur whether the servant is aware of it or not.

The scholars also explain the relationship between the karāmāt of the Awliyāʾ and the miracles of the Prophets through the principle:

كُلُّ كَرَامَةٍ لِوَلِيٍّ فَهِيَ مُعْجِزَةٌ لِنَبِيٍّ

“Every karāmah granted to a walī is, in reality, a miracle belonging to a Prophet.”

Imām al-Nawawī relates the statement from Imām al-Qushayrī رحمه الله that someone might ask how the karāmāt of the Awliyāʾ can appear greater in certain respects than the miracles of the Messengers?

The response is that these karāmāt are connected to the miracles of our Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ. This is because karāmāt cannot occur through someone who is not truthful in his Islam. If a karāmah appears through one of the followers of a Prophet, it is counted among the miracles of that Prophet. Had the Prophet not been truthful, such a karāmah would not have appeared through the one who follows him.

Among the clearest Qurʾānic proofs for the reality of karāmāt is Allah’s account of Maryam: عليها السلام

﴿فَتَقَبَّلَهَا رَبُّهَا بِقَبُولٍ حَسَنٍ وَأَنْبَتَهَا نَبَاتًا حَسَنًا وَكَفَّلَهَا زَكَرِيَّا ۖ كُلَّمَا دَخَلَ عَلَيْهَا زَكَرِيَّا الْمِحْرَابَ وَجَدَ عِندَهَا رِزْقًا ۖ قَالَ يَا مَرْيَمُ أَنَّىٰ لَكِ هَٰذَا ۖ قَالَتْ هُوَ مِنْ عِندِ اللَّهِ ۖ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشَاءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ﴾

“So her Lord accepted her graciously, caused her to grow in a good manner, and placed her under the care of Zakariyyā. Whenever Zakariyyā entered the sanctuary to visit her, he found provision with her. He asked, ‘O Maryam, from where has this come to you?’ She replied, ‘It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without measure.’” Āl ʿImrān 3:37

2. الْمُعْجِزَةُ – The Miracle

A muʿjizah is an extraordinary occurrence that Allah brings about through the hands of a Prophet, accompanied by a claim to Prophethood.

The phrase “accompanied by a claim to prophethood” means that the person through whom the extraordinary occurrence takes place claims to be a Prophet. The claim intended here is a truthful claim to Prophethood. Some scholars also stipulate that the miracle must be accompanied by a challenge to those who deny the prophet’s message.

Our Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ was granted many miracles. Some scholars have stated that they amount to one hundred categories, with numerous individual occurrences falling under each category.

Among them are:

  • تَسْبِيحُ الْحَصَى فِي يَدِهِ – Pebbles glorifying Allah in his hand. This occurred on several occasions.
  • تَكْثِيرُ الطَّعَامِ – The multiplication of food, which also occurred on numerous occasions.
  • نَبْعُ الْمَاءِ مِنْ بَيْنِ أَصَابِعِهِ – Water flowing from between his fingers, which occurred on several occasions.
  • الْإِسْرَاءُ وَالْمِعْرَاجُ – The Night Journey and Ascension.

The greatest of his miracles is الْقُرْآنُ الْكَرِيمُ, which remains an everlasting miracle until the Day of Resurrection. However, the Prophet ﷺ was granted many other miracles, just as the earlier Messengers عليهم الصلاة والسلام were granted miracles.

Allah generally refers to miracles as āyāt (signs), In the Qurʾān, for example, Allah says concerning the she-camel of Ṣāliḥ عليه السلام:

﴿هَٰذِهِ نَاقَةُ اللَّهِ لَكُمْ آيَةً﴾

“This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you.” Hūd 11:64

The scholars later adopted the technical term مُعْجِزَةٌ to refer to these extraordinary signs. There is no objection to the use of this scholarly terminology.

3. الْإِرْهَاصُ – The Irhāṣ

An irhāṣ is an extraordinary occurrence that Allah brings about for a future Prophet before his Prophethood, as a preparation for his future Prophetic mission.

It is not called a muʿjizah because it is not accompanied by a claim to Prophethood.

Examples of those that occurred before the Prophethood of our Messenger Muḥammad ﷺ include:

  • سُجُودُ الشَّجَرِ وَالْحَجَرِ – Trees and stones prostrating before him.
  • إِظْلَالُ الْغَمَامَةِ لَهُ – A cloud shading him.
  • مَيْلَانُ فَيْءِ الشَّجَرَةِ عَلَيْهِ – The shadow of a tree inclining towards him.
  • تَسْلِيمُ الْحَجَرِ عَلَيْهِ – A stone greeting him, with him hearing its greeting.

These occurrences are classified as irhāṣ because they took place before he received Prophethood.

4. الْمَعُونَةُ – Divine Assistance

Maʿūnah is an extraordinary occurrence that appears through some ordinary Muslims or those who are weak in their religious commitment, by which Allah rescues them from hardship, distress, or calamity.

The scholars differed over whether maʿūnah is a category within karāmah or a separate category altogether.

Some scholars consider it a type of karāmah. Others regard it as an independent category because such divine assistance may be granted even to a believer who has not attained the rank of the awliyāʾ and who still possesses shortcomings and weaknesses in faith.

5. الِاسْتِدْرَاجُ وَالْمَكْرُ – Gradual Entrapment and Divine Deception

Istidrāj is an extraordinary occurrence that Allah brings about through the hands of a sinful person, in accordance with what that person desires, as a means of gradually leading him further into misguidance.

The person may begin to believe that he deserves these extraordinary occurrences and that he holds a special status with Allah. As a result, he becomes impressed with himself, while others may also become deceived by what they witness.

Al-Rāzī explains the difference between a karāmah and istidrāj.

The recipient of a true karāmah is never comforted by it. Rather, whenever a karāmah appears, his fear of Allah only increases, for he worries that it may in fact be a form of istidrāj.

As for the recipient of istidrāj, he delights in what appears through him. He imagines that he deserves such favours, begins to look down upon others, grows arrogant, feels secure from Allah’s plan and punishment, and no longer fears an evil end.

Therefore, if such attitudes appear in a person, this indicates that what appeared through him was istidrāj rather than a genuine karāmah.

6. السِّحْرُ – Magic

Siḥr is an extraordinary occurrence that Allah brings about through the hands of a sinful person, allowing him to continue further in his misguidance.

The poet’s expression وَالسِّحْرُ أُتِى indicates that people have resorted to magic. This may involve words they utter or actions they perform while seeking the assistance of the jinn.

7. خَوَارِقُ الدَّجَّالِ – The Extraordinary Occurrences of the Dajjāl

This category refers to the extraordinary occurrences that appear through the Dajjāl and are accompanied by his claim to divinity.

Some scholars classify these occurrences as an independent category because of their immense scale and impact, distinguishing them from the lesser extraordinary occurrences that may appear through others. Other scholars include them under istidrāj.

Allah has made the Dajjāl a trial for mankind. Among the extraordinary occurrences that will appear through him are:

  • He will command the sky to rain, and rain will fall.
  • He will command the earth to produce vegetation, and it will grow.
  • He will kill a man and then bring him back to life.
  • He will pass by a ruined place, and its treasures will follow him like swarms of bees.
  • He will claim to be the Lord, and people will worship him.

Despite these astonishing events, the Prophet ﷺ described him in unmistakable detail, mentioning, among other signs, that he is blind in one eye and that the word “Kāfir” (disbeliever) will be written between his eyes, making his falsehood evident to every true believer.

In light of this description, Imām al-Rāzī explains why the extraordinary occurrences that appear through the Dajjāl do not lead to confusion between him and a true Prophet. He writes:

“Our scholars said: This is permissible because his appearance and physical form indicate his falsehood. Therefore, the appearance of extraordinary occurrences through him does not lead to confusion.”

Among his extraordinary occurrences, the Prophet ﷺ informed us that the Dajjāl will have with him what appears to people as water and fire: “When the Dajjāl emerges, he will have with him water and fire. As for what people see as fire, it will actually be cool water; and as for what people see as cool water, it will actually be fire.”

Among the greatest examples of steadfastness will be the believing man whom the Dajjāl kills and appears to revive. After witnessing this, the believer will only become firmer in his certainty and will proclaim before the people: “You are indeed the False Messiah.”

The Prophet ﷺ said regarding him: “He will be the greatest martyr before the Lord of the worlds.”

8. الْإِهَانَةُ وَالِاحْتِقَارُ – Humiliation and Disgrace

The final category is ihānah, an extraordinary occurrence that Allah brings about through the hands of a sinful person, but in a manner completely contrary to what he intends, thereby humiliating him.

This may occur to someone who falsely claims Prophethood or fights against the religion. Although he seeks to produce extraordinary occurrences to support his claims, what appears through him instead becomes a means of exposing and humiliating him.

Among the famous examples is Musaylimah al-Kadhdhāb. Ibn al-Jawzī relates that whenever he attempted to imitate the miracles of the Prophet ﷺ, the opposite occurred.

A woman once came to Musaylimah and asked him to supplicate to Allah for their date palms and wells, explaining that Muḥammad ﷺ had supplicated for their people and their wells had filled with water.

Musaylimah asked her how the Prophet ﷺ had done this. She explained that he had taken a small amount of water in a bucket, supplicated, rinsed his mouth with it and then spat it back into the water. The people then poured that water into their wells, and the wells filled.

Musaylimah attempted to imitate this. However, when he performed the same action, the water in their wells disappeared.

Another man then brought his child to Musaylimah, asking him to bless the child, since the Prophet ﷺ would bless the children of his Companions. However, every child whose head Musaylimah touched or whose palate he rubbed became afflicted with a speech impediment and lost his hair.

On another occasion, Musaylimah performed wuḍūʾ in a garden and poured the water he had used into it, hoping that it would bring blessing. Yet nothing grew there.

These incidents illustrate what Musaylimah intended as a means of demonstrating his supposed Prophethood became the very means of his humiliation.

Translator’s reflection

One of the greatest gifts of Islamic scholarship is that it teaches us to think with clarity. The extraordinary can easily captivate the imagination. Stories spread quickly, emotions run high, and people often rush to conclusions. Yet the scholars pause and ask: What exactly happened? Through whom? For what purpose? This careful approach is not a lack of spirituality; it is true spirituality. It preserves both our awe of Allah’s power and our commitment to sound belief.

Living this bayt

Our fascination should never stop at the extraordinary. Instead, we should seek understanding.

A believer learns not merely to marvel at remarkable events, but to recognise Allah’s wisdom in every one of them. Knowledge protects the heart from both exaggeration and denial.

verses.tr: Among these extraordinary occurrences are also Istidrāj, magic, the wonders shown by the Dajjāl, and those accompanied by divine humiliation rather than honour.
As for the extraordinary occurrences associated with the people of innovation and the soothsayers, then describe them as satanic phenomena.

exp.en:
The author explains that not every extraordinary occurrence is a كَرَامَةٌ. Some may appear through people of religious innovation, soothsayers, and others who claim knowledge of the unseen. These occurrences are not regarded as karāmāt of the Awliyāʾ. Rather, some scholars call them الحَالُ, or الخارق الشيطاني.

Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah رحمه الله explains that several differences distinguish the genuine karāmāt of the Awliyāʾ from satanic occurrences that may resemble them.

He writes, “As for what occurs at the hands of magicians and soothsayers, it bears no resemblance to the karāmāt of the awliyāʾ. There are many distinctions between the karāmāt of Allah’s friends and those phenomena that resemble them but are in reality satanic.”

He identifies the following distinctions:

  1. Their cause. Karāmāt of the awliyāʾ: They arise from الإيمان والتقوى (faith and consciousness of Allah). Satanic occurrences: They arise from matters prohibited by Allah and His Messenger ﷺ.
  2. Their response to the remembrance of Allah. Karāmāt of the awliyāʾ: They become stronger through the remembrance of Allah and affirming His Oneness. Satanic occurrences: They become weaker or disappear when Allah is remembered, His Oneness is affirmed, and the Qur’an is recited, particularly Āyat al-Kursī, which nullifies most satanic extraordinary occurrences.
  3. Their ability to be matched. Karāmāt of the awliyāʾ: They cannot be opposed or overcome by another occurrence of the same kind or one greater than them. Satanic occurrences: The occurrences performed by magicians, soothsayers, and those who oppose the Messengers can be countered by something similar or even greater.
  4. Their purpose. Karāmāt of the awliyāʾ: Their purpose is عبادة الله وتصديق رسله (worshipping Allah and affirming the truthfulness of His Messengers). They are supporting signs, proofs, and evidence that point towards one truth. Satanic occurrences: Their purpose is الكفر والفسوق والعصيان (disbelief, wickedness and disobedience).

Translator’s reflection

One of the subtle deceptions of Shayṭān is that he does not always invite people to falsehood through obvious evil. Sometimes he cloaks falsehood in the appearance of spirituality. Perhaps the most dangerous mistake a believer can make is confusing power with piety. Shayṭān may assist his allies in astonishing people. Allah honours His allies by drawing them nearer to Him. The two can appear similar to the untrained eye, but they are worlds apart. The first leads to arrogance.

The second leads to humility.

Living this bayt

When confronted with extraordinary claims, do not ask first: “Is it real?” Ask instead: “Where does it lead?” Does it strengthen tawḥīd? Does it increase adherence to the Sunnah? Does it cultivate humility and obedience? Or does it invite people to personalities, hidden knowledge, superstition, and dependence on creation? The destination often reveals the true source.

verses.tr: As for the karāmāt, they encompass every extraordinary event beyond the customary order, whether through an unveiling or by a provision granted by Allah.

exp.en:
Abyāt 12–13

These lines explain that karāmāt are divided into three categories: Kashf (كشف), Rizq (رزق), and Taʾthīr (تأثير). Every extraordinary occurrence granted to the Awliyāʾ falls under one of these three categories.

كَشْفٌ

Literally, unveiling or uncovering. The poet refers to the type of karāmah connected to knowledge, also known as الْمُكَاشَفَاتُ.

The author explains that the karāmāt of the Awliyāʾ fall into three broad categories:

1. الكشف – Unveiling and Extraordinary Knowledge

The first category is الكشف, which refers to a karāmah connected to knowledge. It is also known as المكاشفات.

Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah رحمه الله explains:

“When the heart is filled with taqwā, matters become clear to it and are unveiled. The stronger the faith in the heart, the stronger its ability to perceive matters becomes, and the more it recognises their realities and hidden aspects. Whenever faith weakens, this unveiling also weakens.”

Among the examples of this category are: A servant hearing something that others cannot hear, seeing something that others cannot see, whether while awake or in a dream, or knowing something that others do not know.

One example is الْفِرَاسَةُ الصَّادِقَةُ, truthful insight, through which a person anticipates how certain matters will unfold in the future. This does not mean that a person possesses knowledge of the unseen, for none knows the unseen except Allah. Rather, Allah may honour some of His Awliyāʾ by enabling them to anticipate how events will unfold and then bring those events about as they anticipated.

Examples of this include:

ʿUmar رضي الله عنه was delivering a khuṭbah in Madīnah when he suddenly called out: يَا سَارِيَةُ، الْجَبَلَ “O Sāriyah, the mountain!”

Sāriyah was commanding an army far away. When the army’s messenger later returned, he reported that they had heard a voice calling them to take shelter by the mountain. They did so, and Allah granted them victory. - Al-Bayhaqī, Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwah

As Abū Bakr رضي الله عنه was nearing his death, he explained to his daughter ʿĀʾishah رضي الله عنها how his estate should be divided. He mentioned that her other sibling was the child carried by his wife, Ḥabībah bint Khārijah, and said: ذُو بَطْنِ بِنْتِ خَارِجَةَ، أُرَاهَا جَارِيَةً “The child in the womb of Khārijah’s daughter, whom I believe to be a girl.”

A daughter was subsequently born. - Mālik, al-Muwaṭṭaʾ

During the journey of Mūsā عليه السلام with the righteous servant, the latter killed a young boy. Mūsā عليه السلام questioned this action, but the servant explained that the boy’s parents were righteous believers and that Allah intended to replace him with a child better in purity and affection.

  • قِصَّةُ سَارِيَةَ – The incident involving ʿUmar رضي الله عنه and Sāriyah.
  • إِخْبَارُ أَبِي بَكْرٍ – Abū Bakr رضي الله عنه informing someone that his wife was carrying a female child.
  • إِخْبَارُ عُمَرَ – ʿUmar’sرضي الله عنه prediction concerning one of his descendants who would become a just ruler.
  • قِصَّةُ صَاحِبِ مُوسَى – and the story of the righteous servant who accompanied Mūsā عليه السلام, based on the opinion of those scholars who considered him to be one of the awliyāʾ. The stronger view, however, is that he was himself a prophet.

2. الرزق – Extraordinary Provision

The second category is الرزق, referring to provision extraordinarily granted by Allah.

In such cases, Allah grants one of His righteous servants’ wealth, food, or other forms of sustenance without any apparent worldly means or natural cause. Rather, He extraordinarily provides for them beyond the normal course of events.

The most famous example of this is Maryam عليها السلام, who was repeatedly provided with sustenance from Allah without any visible means.

3. التأثير – Extraordinary Ability and Influence

The third category is التأثير, referring to extraordinary ability and influence granted by Allah to whichever of His Awliyāʾ He wills.

Examples include:

When Khālid ibn al-Walīd رضي الله عنه arrived at al-Ḥīrah and stayed with Banū al-Marāzibah, he was warned that the Persians might give him poison. He asked them to bring it. When it was brought, he placed it in his hand, said بِسْمِ اللهِ, and swallowed it. The poison did not harm him, by Allah’s permission. - Ibn Abī Shaybah, al-Muṣannaf.

When the false prophet al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī demanded that Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī رحمه الله acknowledge his prophethood, Abū Muslim refused and affirmed the Prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ. Al-Aswad ordered a huge fire to be lit and had him thrown into it. However, the fire did not harm him. He was subsequently expelled from Yemen and travelled to Madīnah, where ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رضي الله عنه recognised him, embraced him, and praised Allah for allowing him to witness such an extraordinary occurrence. - Al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ

When al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Ḥaḍramī رضي الله عنه led a Muslim army towards Bahrain, they encountered the sea with no boats available to cross. He supplicated to Allah, asking Him to make a passage for them. Allah enabled the army to cross the water on foot, and they reached the other side safely. - Al-Ṭabarānī, al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr

  • الِاسْتِغْنَاءُ عَنِ الْأَكْلِ وَالشُّرْبِ – Being able to remain without food and drink, as in the story of the People of the Cave.
  • نَقْلُ الشَّيْءِ الثَّقِيلِ فِي لَحَظَاتٍ – Moving something extremely heavy from one place to another in moments, as in the account of the one who possessed knowledge of the Book and brought the throne of Bilqīs from Yemen to Sulaymān عليه السلام in al-Shām.
  • أَكْلُ السُّمِّ دُونَ ضَرَرٍ – Consuming poison without being harmed by it, as in the account of Khālid ibn al-Walīd رضي الله عنه.
  • دُخُولُ النَّارِ دُونَ الِاحْتِرَاقِ – Entering fire without being burned, as in the account of Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī.
  • الْمَشْيُ عَلَى الْمَاءِ – Walking upon water, as in the account of Ibn al-Ḥaḍramī.

Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah رحمه الله writes:

“Among the examples of this are the story of the one who possessed knowledge from the Book, the account of the People of the Cave, the incidents involving Khālid ibn al-Walīd, Safīnah, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī, as well as many others whose explanation would be lengthy. Enumerating such examples would be like attempting to count the raindrops. The purpose here is merely to mention well-known examples familiar to most people. As for divine power that is not directly connected to a person’s own actions, examples include Allah granting victory to those who support His religion and destroying those who revile His awliyāʾ.”

Safīnah رضي الله عنه, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, was once travelling by sea when his ship broke apart. He managed to reach land on a piece of wood, but found himself in an unfamiliar place where a lion approached him. He addressed it, saying: يَا أَبَا الْحَارِثِ، أَنَا مَوْلَى رَسُولِ اللهِ ﷺ “O Abū al-Ḥārith, I am the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.”

The lion lowered its head, approached him, and guided him along the way until he reached the road. It then made a sound, which Safīnah understood as a farewell, before leaving him. - Al-Bayhaqī, Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwah,

The author concludes by explaining that some of these karāmāt serve as مَعُونَةٌ لِلْأَوْلِيَاءِ فِي الدِّينِ وَالدُّنْيَا (assistance to the Awliyāʾ in religious and worldly matters).

In religious matters, Allah may assist them in:

  • الْجِهَادِ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ – Striving in the path of Allah.
  • الدَّعْوَةِ إِلَى اللَّهِ – Calling others towards Allah.
  • تَبْلِيغِ الدِّينِ – Conveying the religion.
  • الِاجْتِهَادِ فِي الْعِبَادَةِ – Striving in worship.

Allah may also assist them in their worldly affairs. Thus, He grants assistance to the people of taqwā in both their religious and worldly lives.

Translator’s reflection

Perhaps the most beautiful lesson of this bayt is that Allah’s care for His servants is not confined to one form. Sometimes He honours them with knowledge they could never have acquired on their own. At other times, He provides for them from avenues they never imagined. In every case, the focus remains the same: not the servant, but the Lord who honoured him. The believer, therefore, does not seek kashf. He seeks closeness to Allah. He does not chase extraordinary provision. He places his trust in Ar-Razzāq, knowing that every gift arrives only by His decree.

Living this bayt

Many believers wait for dramatic signs from Allah. Yet Allah’s greatest gifts often arrive quietly. A difficulty suddenly lifted. A door unexpectedly opened. Knowledge granted at the moment it is needed. Strength placed in the heart when everything else seems to fail. Whether public or private, every true karāmah points not to the servant, but to the generosity of Allah.

verses.tr: Or it may appear as divine assistance granted to Allah’s righteous friends, through which they are aided in matters of both their religion and their worldly affairs; for it is the people of taqwā whom Allah supports.
Know with certainty that the noblest of all miracles is to worship Allah with unwavering steadfastness.

exp.en:
This verse may rightly be described as the very heart of the poem, for it contains the single most important principle every Muslim should understand regarding the karāmāt of the Awliyāʾ: a Walī of Allah possesses īmān and taqwā, and attaining the status of Wilāyah does not depend on experiencing an extraordinary occurrence.

The poet expresses this principle beautifully:

فَأَكْرَمُ الْكَرَامَةِ لُزُومُ الِاسْتِقَامَةِ

The greatest karāmah is to remain steadfast upon the obedience of Allah.

This meaning has also been reported from some of the early generations. Every Walī of Allah possesses the karāmah of steadfastness upon the truth. However, a karāmah in the sense of an extraordinary occurrence that breaks the customary order of things may happen to some Awliyāʾ and not to others.

Many of the greatest Companions رضي الله عنهمand leading scholars, whose righteousness and religious standing are unanimously recognised, have no recorded accounts of extraordinary occurrences, while such occurrences have been reported from people of a lesser rank.

The position of Ahl al-Sunnah and the Salaf: it is not necessary for every Walī of Allah to experience a supernatural occurrence. Indeed, many of the finest Awliyāʾ of Allah, particularly among the most distinguished Companions, have no recorded karāmāt of this nature.

Conversely, extraordinary phenomena may also appear at the hands of magicians, fortune-tellers, impostors, sinners, and even unbelievers.

Imām al-Layth ibn Saʿd رحمه الله said:

إِذَا رَأَيْتُمُ الرَّجُلَ يَمْشِي عَلَى الْمَاءِ فَلَا تَغْتَرُّوا بِهِ حَتَّى تَعْرِضُوا أَمْرَهُ عَلَى الْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ.

“If you see a man walking upon water, do not be deceived by him until you have measured his conduct against the Qur’an and Sunnah.”

When this statement was conveyed to Imām al-Shāfiʿī رحمه الله, he remarked:

قَصَّرَ اللَّيْثُ، لَوْ رَأَيْتُمُ الرَّجُلَ يَمْشِي عَلَى الْمَاءِ وَيَطِيرُ فِي الْهَوَاءِ فَلَا تَغْتَرُّوا بِهِ حَتَّى تَعْرِضُوا أَمْرَهُ عَلَى الْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ.

“Al-Layth understated the matter! Even if you see a man walking upon water and flying through the air, do not be deceived by him until you have measured his conduct against the Qur’an and Sunnah.”

The example of al-Masīḥ al-Dajjāl further demonstrates this principle. Despite being an enemy of Allah and one of the leaders of disbelief, he will perform extraordinary acts. He will command the sky to send down rain, and it will rain; he will command the earth to produce vegetation, and it will do so. He will pass through a ruined place, and its treasures will follow him like swarms of bees. He will also kill a man and then bring him back to life by Allah’s permission. Despite these extraordinary occurrences, he remains an enemy of Allah who falsely claims divinity.

Therefore, an extraordinary occurrence is not, in itself, evidence of a person’s righteousness or faith.

The correct approach is the opposite: when a person is already known for his righteousness, sound belief and steadfast adherence to the Sharīʿah, and an extraordinary occurrence takes place through him, it may then be regarded as a karāmah with which Allah has honoured him.

Some who deviated among the Ṣūfiyyah, however, adopted the mistaken approach of treating extraordinary occurrences as proof of a person’s Wilāyah, regardless of his outward conduct. They would cite accounts found in works such as al-Shaʿrānī’s Ṭabaqāt al-Awliyāʾ and similar writings, presenting extraordinary occurrences as evidence of sainthood even when the person’s apparent condition was marked by corruption and deviation. This is an error and a form of misguidance.

Such occurrences may instead be the result of magic and the assistance of the jinn, through which people are deceived and led astray. They are not karāmāt.

The correct measure is therefore clear: a person is among the Awliyāʾ of Allah because of his īmān, taqwā, and steadfastness upon obedience, whether an extraordinary occurrence takes place through him or not. If such an occurrence does happen, it is an additional honour from Allah; it is not what establishes his Wilāyah.

Translator’s reflection

This may be the most liberating lesson in the entire poem. Many people spend their lives searching for signs, extraordinary experiences, and stories that amaze the mind. Yet the greatest gift Allah can bestow upon a servant is far quieter: to wake every morning with faith in the heart, sincerity in the intention, and the strength to obey Him once again.

A lifetime of consistent prayer is a greater miracle than a moment of public wonder.

Living this bayt

Do not ask Allah for extraordinary experiences. Ask Him for extraordinary steadfastness. Ask Him to preserve your prayer, your sincerity, your Qur’an, your manners, your tawḥīd, your love of the Sunnah, until your final breath. If Allah grants you that... you have already received the greatest karāmah.

verses.tr: At times, Allah may grant a karāmah to one whose faith has become weak, purely as an act of divine grace, lest he deviate from the straight path.

exp.en:
In this verse, the author highlights an important subtlety in the subject of karāmāt.

Allah, in His wisdom and mercy, may sometimes honour a believer whose faith is relatively weak with an extraordinary occurrence to strengthen his conviction, increase his certainty, and keep him firm upon the path of Islam.

Meanwhile, another person who is among the finest of the righteous may be left to rely upon the strength of his own faith, without experiencing any extraordinary occurrence.

As discussed earlier, when an extraordinary occurrence takes place through someone who is sinful or has fallen into wrongdoing, and it serves to strengthen his faith and establish him firmly upon Islam, the scholars refer to it as الْمَعُونَةُ (divine assistance).

This demonstrates that the occurrence of a karāmah is not necessarily an indication that one servant is superior to another. On the contrary, it may sometimes be granted precisely because a person’s faith requires reinforcement, whereas those whose faith is already deeply rooted are sustained by the strength of their certainty alone.

This principle perfectly complements the previous verse: the highest honour is not witnessing miracles but remaining steadfast without needing them.

Translator’s reflection

One of the most comforting truths in this poem is that Allah knows the condition of every heart. Some servants advance through unwavering consistency. Others stumble, weaken, and fear that they may lose their way. Yet Allah, in His perfect wisdom, nurtures each soul according to its need. At times, He grants a servant an unexpected reassurance, not because that servant has reached a higher station, but because Allah wishes to preserve him from falling further.

Living this bayt

There is immense comfort here. Every believer experiences moments of weakness. When Allah strengthens your heart after hardship, opens a door when everything seemed closed, or grants you a renewed love for worship after a period of dryness, recognise these moments as gifts from His mercy. But do not become attached to the gift. Become attached to the Giver.

verses.tr: Karāmāt are most found among those devoted to the worship of Allah, and they are also frequently witnessed in the arenas of jihād in His cause.

exp.en:
Abyāt 16–19

The poet now turns to an important distinction between the people of knowledge and those devoted primarily to worship. He explains that karāmāt are more commonly found among the العُبَّادِ (those devoted to worship) and those engaged in الجِهَادِ, while they are less commonly found among the العُلَمَاءِ (scholars).

This observation is mentioned by Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah and other leading scholars. However, the poet is not suggesting that a worshipper who performs abundant voluntary acts of worship is superior to a scholar simply because extraordinary occurrences may appear through him.

Rather, the poet explains:

فَالْعِلْمُ حَسْبُ الْعُلَمَاءِ هَادِيًا

Knowledge is sufficient to guide the scholars.

The scholars possess beneficial knowledge that strengthens them in the truth and guides their actions. They are therefore not in the same need of extraordinary occurrences to strengthen their faith as others may be.

This distinction is illustrated by the famous narration concerning a man who travelled from Madīnah to Damascus to meet Abū al-Dardāʾ رضي الله عنه. When Abū al-Dardāʾ asked him what had brought him there, the man explained that he had come solely to learn a ḥadīth that had reached him from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Abū al-Dardāʾ then narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

مَنْ سَلَكَ طَرِيقًا يَبْتَغِي فِيهِ عِلْمًا، سَلَكَ اللَّهُ بِهِ طَرِيقًا إِلَى الْجَنَّةِ، وَإِنَّ الْمَلَائِكَةَ لَتَضَعُ أَجْنِحَتَهَا رِضًا لِطَالِبِ الْعِلْمِ، وَإِنَّ الْعَالِمَ لَيَسْتَغْفِرُ لَهُ مَنْ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَنْ فِي الْأَرْضِ، حَتَّى الْحِيتَانُ فِي الْمَاءِ، وَفَضْلُ الْعَالِمِ عَلَى الْعَابِدِ كَفَضْلِ الْقَمَرِ عَلَى سَائِرِ الْكَوَاكِبِ، إِنَّ الْعُلَمَاءَ وَرَثَةُ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ، إِنَّ الْأَنْبِيَاءَ لَمْ يُوَرِّثُوا دِينَارًا وَلَا دِرْهَمًا، إِنَّمَا وَرَّثُوا الْعِلْمَ، فَمَنْ أَخَذَ بِهِ أَخَذَ بِحَظٍّ وَافِرٍ.

“Whoever travels a path seeking knowledge, Allah will make easy for him a path to Paradise. Indeed, the angels lower their wings out of pleasure with the seeker of knowledge. The inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, even the fish in the water, seek forgiveness for the scholar. The superiority of a scholar over a worshipper is like the superiority of the moon over the rest of the stars. Indeed, the scholars are the heirs of the Prophets. The Prophets did not leave behind dinars or dirhams; rather, they left behind knowledge. Whoever takes hold of it has indeed taken hold of an abundant share.” Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah

The poet then highlights another distinction: A scholar who leaves behind beneficial knowledge is granted a good mention among people, while the reward of his knowledge continues even after his death. His teachings continue to benefit others, and his reward continues to increase through that benefit.

As for why karāmāt are more commonly found among worshippers and those engaged in jihād, while they are less common among scholars, the explanation drawn from the words of Shaykh al-Islām and other scholars is that one of the purposes of a karāmah is التَّثْبِيتُ (strengthening and keeping a person firm upon the truth). Those devoted to worship and jihād who possess a lesser share of beneficial knowledge may need such occurrences to strengthen them in the good they are doing. As for the scholars, Allah has already granted them beneficial knowledge through which they are strengthened and guided, making them less dependent upon extraordinary occurrences.

Translator’s reflection

Among the greatest aspirations of a believer is not merely to leave this world with good deeds, but to leave behind deeds that continue to bear fruit after he has departed. This is one of the quiet miracles of sacred knowledge. Death silences the tongue, but it cannot silence beneficial knowledge. Every time someone learns from it, acts upon it, or teaches it to another, the reward ascends once again.

The believer should therefore ask not only, “What am I doing today?” but also, “What am I building that will continue to serve Allah’s religion after I am gone?“

Living this bayt

Ask yourself: If I were to return to Allah tonight... What would continue after me? A lesson? A student? A translation? A child? A book? A sincere piece of advice? This bayt invites us to live for the kind of deeds that outlive us.

verses.tr: Karāmāt seldom appear among the scholars, for the knowledge they possess is itself sufficient to guide them.
The superiority of the scholar, as authentically reported in the Prophetic tradition, over the devoted worshipper is like the superiority of the full moon over the rest of the stars.
He is blessed with an honourable remembrance among the people, while his reward continues to endure. It does not cease with his death; rather, it continues to increase.
Those who denied the reality of the karāmāt were the people of the Muʿtazilah and the adherents of philosophical speculation, the people of misguidance.

exp.en:
Abyāt 20–21

The poet now turns to those who deny the karāmāt of the Awliyāʾ, identifying the Muʿtazilah and the philosophers among those who have gone astray in this matter. He rejects the claim that extraordinary occurrences granted to people other than Prophets would become indistinguishable from the miracles of Prophets.

Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah رحمه الله explains that several groups deviated in this subject.

1. Those who deny extraordinary occurrences outside Prophethood

One group claimed that an extraordinary occurrence can only take place through a Prophet. Consequently, they rejected the reports of extraordinary occurrences involving magicians, soothsayers and the righteous Awliyāʾ.

Shaykh al-Islām identifies this as the position of most of the Muʿtazilah, as well as others such as Abū Muḥammad ibn Ḥazm.

Their reasoning was that if extraordinary occurrences could happen through someone who was not a Prophet, there would be no distinguishing feature between a Prophet and anyone else. According to their position, the only thing that distinguished a Prophet was the occurrence of extraordinary events through him.

2. Those who make no distinction between the different types of extraordinary occurrences

Another group went to the opposite extreme. They maintained that all such occurrences are possible without restriction. Whatever extraordinary occurrence takes place through a Prophet could also take place through a righteous person, a magician, or a soothsayer.

According to this group, the distinction is not in the extraordinary occurrence itself, but in what accompanies it: the Prophet makes a claim to Prophethood and challenges others through it.

3. The philosophers and their explanation of extraordinary occurrences

Shaykh al-Islām also mentions the mulḥid philosophers who explain extraordinary occurrences through what they call:

  • الْقُوَى الْفَلَكِيَّةُ – Celestial powers.
  • الْقُوَى النَّفْسَانِيَّةُ – Psychic powers.
  • الْقُوَى الطَّبِيعِيَّةُ – Natural powers.

In other words, they acknowledge that extraordinary occurrences take place, but attribute them to celestial, psychic, and natural forces rather than recognising them as a karāmah granted by Allah to His Awliyāʾ.

Their position therefore ultimately leads to denying the karāmah according to the understanding of Ahl al-Sunnah wa’l-Jamāʿah.

The balanced position of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamāʿah rejects all these extremes. They affirm that miraculous events may occur for the awliyāʾ of Allah, but only by Allah’s permission and as an honour bestowed upon His righteous servants. At the same time, they distinguish these karāmāt from prophetic miracles, satanic deceptions, sorcery, and other forms of extraordinary occurrences, each of which has its own characteristics and purpose.

Translator’s reflection

This bayt teaches a wider principle. Many theological errors arise because people assume that if two things share one characteristic, they must be identical. Yet Islam constantly distinguishes between things that resemble one another in one respect while differing completely in purpose and rank.

Similarity is not identity.

Living this bayt

The believer today may never encounter classical Muʿtazilah, but he may encounter the same way of thinking. Whenever someone says: “I cannot accept this because my mind cannot comprehend it,” he should remember that revelation informs us about realities beyond the limits of our perception. Faith does not ask us to abandon reason. It asks us to place reason in its rightful place: as a servant of revelation, not its master.

verses.tr: They claimed that affirming the karāmāt would blur the distinction between them and the miracles of the Prophets. Yet I say: this is nothing but a clear and fundamental error.
The distinction between a prophetic miracle and a karāmah is that the former accompanies a claim to Prophethood and serves to manifest and confirm that divine message.

exp.en:
The difference between a miracle (Muʿjizah) given to a Prophet and an extraordinary occurrence (Karāmah) granted to a righteous servant of Allah lies in the following:

1. The Claim of Prophethood

A Muʿjizah is accompanied by a claim of prophethood. The Prophet declares that he is a Messenger of Allah, and the miracle serves as a sign supporting his claim. A Walī, however, does not claim to be a Prophet or Messenger. A Karāmah does not make someone a Prophet.

2. Challenging Others

Prophets present their miracles as proof of their prophethood and challenge those who reject their message. A Walī, on the other hand, does not seek to display his Karāmah or challenge people with it. Any extraordinary event that occurs at his hands is not intended to prove a divine message, nor does he present it as evidence of any special rank. Rather, it is a favour and honour bestowed upon him by Allah alone.

3. The Attitude Towards a Karāmah

A righteous person may fear that displaying a Karāmah will lead to pride, self-admiration (ʿUjb) or a trial for himself. For this reason, he does not seek to make such occurrences known.

Only in exceptional circumstances might a saint reveal a karāmah, for example, when doing so would clearly benefit Islam, strengthen people’s faith, support the religion, or assist in calling others to Allah. Even then, this is done out of necessity and not out of a desire for recognition.

In many cases, a karāmah occurs without the saint intending it or even expecting it, demonstrating that it is purely an act of Allah’s grace rather than something the servant controls or seeks.

Translator’s reflection

There is a lesson here that extends beyond the discussion of karāmāt. Islam teaches us to judge matters not merely by how they appear, but by why they exist.

Purpose often reveals what appearance cannot.

The same outward act may carry entirely different meanings depending upon its intention and function.

Living this bayt

The believer learns to appreciate precision. Not every similarity means equality. Not every extraordinary event carries the same significance. Knowledge protects us from confusion by teaching us the distinctions that revelation itself makes. This is why learning ʿaqīdah is so important. It trains the believer to think with clarity and balance.

verses.tr: Karāmāt are of two categories: one is the greater type, while the other comprises the lesser forms ordinarily bestowed upon the righteous servant.

exp.en:
The author explains that prophetic miracles (muʿjizāt) may be viewed as two broad categories.

1. The major miracles (المعجزات الكبرى)

The major miracles (المعجزات الكبرى) are unique to the Prophets and can never occur at the hands of a non-prophet. They are extraordinary signs that establish the truthfulness of prophethood and cannot be equalled by anyone else.

2. The minor miracles (المعجزات الصغرى)

The minor miracles (المعجزات الصغرى), however, are miracles whose type or genus may also occur for the righteous servants of Allah. When such extraordinary events occur for one of the Awliyāʾ, they are no longer called muʿjizāt but are instead termed karāmāt (honours bestowed by Allah upon His righteous servants).

This distinction safeguards the unique rank of prophethood while affirming the reality of the karāmāt of the Awliyāʾ, which are unanimously accepted by Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamāʿah.

Translator’s reflection

There is a subtle educational lesson here. People naturally focus on visible things. The scholars first teach us to value the invisible. Steadfastness, knowledge, and sincerity. Only then do they discuss extraordinary outward events.

Islam consistently trains the heart before it fascinates the eye.

Living this bayt

Every believer should ask himself: Am I pursuing the greater gifts of Allah, or merely admiring the lesser ones?

If Allah grants you sincerity, steadfastness, beneficial knowledge, and a heart attached to Him, you have already received treasures greater than many of the extraordinary events that capture people’s imagination.

verses.tr: The first category is that Allah grants His righteous servant a distinction whose rank and nature can never be confused with prophetic miracles. Reflect upon this carefully.

exp.en:
The author now introduces an important qualification. Although certain karāmāt may outwardly resemble the great miracles of the Prophets, they can never equal them.

If Allah grants one of His righteous servants an extraordinary event that appears similar to a major prophetic miracle, it will always remain lesser in both degree and quality. The resemblance is only in kind, not in rank, scope, or perfection.

For this reason, scholars explain that while the Awliyāʾ may experience miracles resembling the Prophets’ minor miracles, the major miracles, which establish prophethood and manifest Allah’s decisive proof, remain the exclusive distinction of the Messengers.

Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah رحمه الله highlighted this principle, stating that the signs of the Prophets by which their prophethood is established are far greater than the extraordinary matters shared between the Prophets and their righteous followers. The miracles that serve as proofs of prophethood occupy a rank that no karāmah can attain.

This distinction preserves both beliefs simultaneously: the affirmation of the karāmāt of the Awliyāʾ and the unique, unsurpassed status of the muʿjizāt of the Prophets.

Translator’s reflection

Shaykh Waleed is teaching us to become precise thinkers. The careless mind sees two extraordinary events and says: “They are the same.” The trained mind asks: Who received them? Why were they given? What purpose do they serve? What is their rank?

Knowledge begins with asking the right questions.

Living this bayt

In every area of life, appearances can deceive. Islam teaches us to look beyond the surface. The believer learns not only to ask: “What happened?” but also: “Why did Allah allow it to happen?” Understanding purpose often reveals truths that appearances conceal.

verses.tr: Indeed, every karāmah granted to the Awliyāʾ should be regarded as one of the miracles of the Prophets whom they follow.

exp.en:
Abyāt 25–26

Continuing from the distinction between the miracles of Prophets and the karāmāt of the Awliyāʾ, the poet now establishes an important principle: every karāmah granted to a Walī is, in reality, a miracle for the Prophet whom he follows.

Allah تعالى honours the Awliyāʾ with these extraordinary occurrences because of their adherence to the teachings of their Prophets.

Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah رحمه الله explains that these karāmāt occur through the blessing of following the Messenger ﷺ:

“These karāmāt have only occurred through the blessing of following His Messenger.”

They are therefore among the signs that demonstrate the truthfulness of the Messenger whom these Awliyāʾ follow. Some of the signs given to Prophets may also appear through their followers. When this happens, the occurrence itself remains connected to the truthfulness of the Prophet, since it appears through those who believe in his Prophethood.

The scholars have also observed that every miracle bestowed upon a previous Prophet was granted to our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in an even greater form, either directly as one of his own miracles or indirectly as a karāmah granted to one of the righteous members of his Ummah.
