In both cases, they ultimately testify to the greatness and truthfulness of the final Messenger ﷺ.

One striking example is the miracle of Mūsā عليه السلام, who struck a rock with his staff and twelve springs gushed forth. By contrast, water flowed directly from between the blessed fingers of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, providing enough water for an entire army. This miracle is even more extraordinary, for while water naturally emerges from rocks, it does not emerge from human fingers.

Likewise, the fire becoming cool and safe for Ibrāhīm عليه السلام was among his miracles. A similar occurrence took place as a karāmah for Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī رحمه الله, when he was cast into a fire without being harmed.

Similarly, the parting of the sea for Mūsā عليه السلام found its counterpart in the crossing of the sea by al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Ḥaḍramī رضي الله عنهand his army, while reports also mention that miracles resembling the raising of the dead, granted to ʿĪsā عليه السلام, occurred as karāmāt for some of the Companions and Tābiʿūn.

These examples beautifully illustrate that the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ inherited not prophethood, but the blessings of following the Seal of the Prophets. Every karāmah granted to a believer ultimately points back to the greatness of the Messenger ﷺ, through whose guidance Allah honoured this Ummah.

Translator’s reflection

This bayt transforms our understanding of spiritual rank. The greatest Awliyāʾ never point people towards themselves. Their very existence points back to the Messenger ﷺ. If a person’s extraordinary experiences make people admire him more than they admire the Sunnah, then something has gone terribly wrong.

The true walī becomes a signpost. He does not say: “Look at me.” He says:”Follow the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.”

Living this bayt

Whenever you hear of a righteous person’s steadfastness or an authentic karāmah, let it strengthen your love for the Prophet ﷺ. The saint’s honour is not an alternative path. It is evidence of the power of the prophetic path. Every genuine karāmah whispers the same message: “The way of the Messenger ﷺ is true.”

verses.tr: That is, I mean the Prophets who were sent to those very righteous servants; it was through following those Prophets that they were honoured by Allah.
Furthermore, the Book of our Lord has clearly established that extraordinary occurrences were indeed granted to righteous people among the nations before us.

exp.en:
Abyāt 27–28

The author now establishes that the Qur’an itself provides evidence for the occurrence of خَوَارِقِ الْعَادَةِ among the righteous people who came before us. He gives two examples: the prolonged sleep of the People of the Cave and the extraordinary provision granted to Maryam عليها السلام.

1. The Prolonged Sleep of the People of the Cave

The People of the Cave remained asleep inside the cave for three hundred years, with an additional nine years. Allah says:

﴿وَلَبِثُوا فِي كَهْفِهِمْ ثَلَاثَ مِائَةٍ سِنِينَ وَازْدَادُوا تِسْعًا﴾

“And they remained in their cave for three hundred years, and added nine.” Al-Kahf 18:25

During this time, Allah caused their bodies to turn from side to side, onto their right and left.

Their prolonged sleep over such an extraordinary period is one of the examples the author presents as evidence of a khāriq al-ʿādah (an occurrence beyond the customary order of things).

2. The Provision Granted to Maryam عليها السلام

Maryam bint ʿImrān عليها السلام was granted a karāmah in the form of extraordinary provision.

Whenever Zakariyyā عليه السلام entered the miḥrāb to visit her, he found fruits with her that were out of season: summer fruits during winter and winter fruits during summer. No one had brought these provisions to her.

Allah says:

﴿كُلَّمَا دَخَلَ عَلَيْهَا زَكَرِيَّا الْمِحْرَابَ وَجَدَ عِندَهَا رِزْقًا﴾

“Whenever Zakariyyā entered the sanctuary to visit her, he found provision with her.” Āl ʿImrān 3:37

Surprised by this, Zakariyyā عليه السلام asked her:

﴿يَا مَرْيَمُ أَنَّىٰ لَكِ هَٰذَا﴾

“O Maryam, from where has this come to you?”

She replied:

﴿قَالَتْ هُوَ مِنْ عِندِ اللَّهِ ۖ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشَاءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ﴾

“She said, ‘It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without measure.’” Āl ʿImrān 3:37

The author concludes by clarifying that Maryam عليها السلام was not a Prophet, according to the position held by the majority of scholars, who maintain that Prophets were exclusively men and that there were no female Prophets.

Thus, the two examples demonstrate different forms of extraordinary occurrences: the People of the Cave experienced an extraordinary extension of sleep, while Maryam عليها السلام extraordinarily received provision. Both are established through the Qur’an as examples of Allah’s extraordinary favour upon His righteous servants.

Translator’s reflection

This bayt reminds us of an important principle: A believer does not build his creed upon remarkable stories circulating among people. He builds it upon revelation. Once the Qurʾān establishes something, the believer accepts it with certainty, even if it lies beyond his ordinary experience.

Living this bayt

In an age where extraordinary claims are often exaggerated or fabricated, this bayt teaches us to ask: What has Allah affirmed? Not every astonishing story deserves belief. But what Allah has narrated in His Book is beyond doubt. The believer’s certainty is anchored in revelation, not sensationalism.

verses.sadr: مِنۡ ذَاكَ طُولُ نَوۡمِ أَهۡلِ الۡكَهۡفِ
verses.tr: Among these are the prolonged sleep of the Companions of the Cave and the wondrous provision bestowed upon Maryam, supplied with every kind of sustenance by her Lord.
Our Lord inspired the mother of the One who spoke to Him directly, revealing to her with certainty that her son would be safe, for he would become a Messenger of Allah.

exp.en:
The poet now gives another example: الكَشْفُ, a form of karāmah connected to knowledge. Allah granted this honour to the mother of Mūsā عليه السلام, a righteous woman from Banū Isrāʾīl.

Allah says:

﴿وَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَىٰ أُمِّ مُوسَىٰ أَنْ أَرْضِعِيهِ ۖ فَإِذَا خِفْتِ عَلَيْهِ فَأَلْقِيهِ فِي الْيَمِّ وَلَا تَخَافِي وَلَا تَحْزَنِي ۖ إِنَّا رَادُّوهُ إِلَيْكِ وَجَاعِلُوهُ مِنَ الْمُرْسَلِينَ﴾

“We inspired the mother of Mūsā: ‘Nurse him, but when you fear for him, place him in the river. Do not fear, nor grieve. We shall surely return him to you and make him one of the Messengers.’” Al-Qaṣaṣ 28:7

Allah inspired her with the knowledge that her child would be safe, that he would be returned to her, and that he would eventually become one of His Messengers.

This was a remarkable form of كَشْفٍ, as Allah informed her of something that was hidden from her: the future of her child. It was a karāmah granted to a righteous woman, not revelation of Prophethood.

The poet therefore uses this incident as another Qur’anic example of a karāmah involving knowledge.

Translator’s reflection

Notice the emotional beauty of this story. Allah did not remove the trial. She still had to place her child into the river. What He removed was fear. Sometimes Allah changes our circumstances. Sometimes He changes our hearts so that we can endure them.

Living this bayt

There are moments when obedience to Allah seems to run against every worldly instinct. The mother of Mūsā teaches us that complete trust in Allah often means taking the step He commands before we can see the wisdom behind it. Faith does not always remove uncertainty from the road. It removes uncertainty about the One guiding the road.

verses.tr: Likewise, the Sunnah and transmitted reports contain accounts of such extraordinary occurrences. How beautiful are the narrated reports!

exp.en:
Abyāt 30–31

The poet now moves from the examples of karāmāt mentioned in the Qur’an to those recorded in the Sunnah and transmitted reports (الآثار). He mentions two incidents involving the Companions رضي الله عنهم.

1. The blessing in Abū Bakr’s food

The first incident concerns Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq رضي الله عنه. This account is recorded in both Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim.

He once took three guests to his home. Whenever they ate a morsel from the bowl, more food appeared beneath it than had been there before. The guests all ate until they were satisfied, yet when Abū Bakr and his wife looked at the bowl, they found that it contained even more food than before. He then brought it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and many others came and ate from it until they were all satisfied.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhumā) narrated that the People of the Ṣuffah were poor, and the Prophet ﷺ said:

“Whoever has food enough for two should take a third with him, and whoever has enough for four should take a fifth or a sixth.”

Abū Bakr took three guests to his house while the Prophet ﷺ took ten. Abū Bakr remained with the Prophet ﷺ until after the ʿIshāʾ prayer and returned home late. His wife asked what had delayed him from his guests. He asked whether they had been served, and she replied that they had refused to eat until he arrived. When he finally encouraged them to eat, every time they took a morsel, more food appeared beneath it. After everyone had eaten their fill, the food in the bowl had increased rather than decreased. Abū Bakr looked at it and found it to be as much as before, or even more. He carried it to the Prophet ﷺ, and later many more people ate from it as well.

This was a karāmah in which Allah placed extraordinary blessing and increase in Abū Bakr’s food.

2. The provision given to Khubayb ibn ʿAdī

The second incident concerns Khubayb ibn ʿAdī رضي الله عنه, a noble Companion who was held captive by the disbelievers in Makkah.

During his captivity, he would be provided with fresh grapes to eat. Yet, at that time, there was not a single grape in Makkah.

Whenever his captors entered the place where he was being held, they would find grapes with him, which he would eat.

This was another karāmah: Allah provided Khubayb رضي الله عنه with food that was not ordinarily available in Makkah at that time.

Translator’s reflection

There is something deeply comforting about Khubayb’s story. Outwardly, everything suggested abandonment. He was imprisoned. Awaiting execution. Far from his family. Yet Allah honoured him with provision that no jailer could explain. Sometimes Allah does not remove the prison. He simply reminds His servant that even inside the prison, he remains under divine care. That lesson extends far beyond physical imprisonment. Many believers today feel trapped by illness, hardship, grief, or uncertainty. Khubayb reminds us that Allah’s provision reaches places where human means cannot.

Living this bayt

True barakah is not measured by quantity but by Allah’s blessing.

A small meal may satisfy many. A simple income may carry immense goodness. Likewise, our circumstances do not determine Allah’s care for us. Whether we experience ease or hardship, abundance or restriction, His provision reaches His servants in the manner and at the time He knows to be best.

verses.tr: Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq was blessed with increase in his food, and Khubayb received provision while held in captivity.”
An oath was fulfilled for ibn Mālik, while Khālid remained unharmed after consuming poison.

exp.en:
The poet now mentions two further accounts of karāmāt involving the Companions رضي الله عنهم: the answered supplication of al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik and the incident of Khālid ibn al-Walīd رضي الله عنه drinking poison without being harmed.

1. The answered oath of al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik

The first incident concerns al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik رضي الله عنه, a noble Companion. He was known for making an oath when supplicating to Allah, and Allah would fulfil it.

It is reported that when the fighting became difficult for the Muslims during Jihād, they would call out to him: “O Barāʾ, make an oath by your Lord!”

He would then supplicate: “My Lord, I beseech You by this oath to grant us victory over them.”

The enemy would then be defeated.

During the Battle of Tustar, Barāʾ رضي الله عنه made the following supplication: “My Lord, I beseech You to grant us victory over them and make me the first martyr.”

Allah granted them victory, and al-Barāʾ رضي الله عنه was was honoured with martyrdom.

2. Khālid ibn al-Walīd drinking poison

The second incident concerns Khālid ibn al-Walīd رضي الله عنه. This account is mentioned by a number of scholars and in several works, including Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal’s Faḍāʾil al-Ṣaḥābah, al-Ṭabarānī’s al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr, and Ibn ʿAsākir’s Tārīkh Dimashq.

Ibn ʿAsākir relates that after Khālid ibn al-Walīd returned from the Battle of al-Yamāmah, his army camped at a place called al-Jurʿah, between al-Ḥīrah and the river. The people of al-Ḥīrah fortified themselves in their castles and pelted the Muslims with stones until they ran out, after which they began throwing broken pottery.

Ḍirār ibn al-Azwar remarked, “They have no greater strategy than what you see.”

Khālid then requested that they send one of their wise men to speak with him. They sent ʿAbd al-Masīḥ ibn ʿAmr ibn Qays ibn Ḥayyān ibn Buqaylah al-Ghassānī, who was then three hundred and fifty years old. As he approached Khālid, he was holding poison in his hand.

Khālid asked, “What is that in your hand?”

He replied, “Poison.”

Khālid asked, “What do you intend to do with it?”

He answered, “If I find from you what pleases my people and me, I will praise Allah. Otherwise, I will not be the first to bring humiliation and calamity upon them. I shall drink it and find relief, for little remains of my life.”

Khālid said, “Give it to me.”

When it was placed in his hand, Khālid said:

“In the Name of Allah and by Allah. O Lord of the earth and the heavens, in whose Name no illness can cause harm.”

He then drank the poison. He briefly became faint, struck his chin against his chest, perspired heavily, and then recovered completely.

ʿAbd al-Masīḥ returned to his people and said:

“I have come from a man who is like no ordinary human. He drank deadly poison and it did not harm him. Make peace with him.”

They subsequently agreed to a treaty for one hundred thousand.

Some narrations add that the people had challenged Khālid, saying:

“We will not surrender until you drink this poison.”

Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah said that some of the early scholars cited this incident as a sign of the truthfulness of Islam and the prophethood of the Messenger ﷺ. He also mentioned that Khālid drank the poison when asked to produce a sign, and it caused him no harm.

He further wrote that Khālid once besieged a strongly fortified fortress, whose people declared:

“We will not surrender until you drink the poison.”

So, he drank it, and it did not harm him.

If this report is authentic, then Khālid’s drinking of the poison was an act of complete trust and reliance upon Allah, intended to support the religion of Allah, strike fear into the hearts of the disbelievers, and strengthen the faith of the Muslims. It may therefore be regarded as one of his karāmāt, or perhaps Khālid had received specific guidance from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in this matter, as Ibn Ḥajar suggested in Fatḥ al-Bārī.

Translator’s reflection

There is a subtle lesson here. People often think the greatest miracle is changing the world around them. But Barā’s (RA) story reminds us that the greatest honour is having such sincerity and trust in Allah that one’s supplication is beloved to Him. Likewise, Khālid’s (RA) story reminds us that courage does not come from believing oneself invincible. It comes from believing that one’s life rests entirely in Allah’s hands.

Living this bayt

The believer should strive not for extraordinary experiences, but for extraordinary trust in Allah. If Allah grants acceptance of one’s duʿāʾ, that is a gift. If He grants protection in times of danger, that too is a gift. In both cases, the servant attributes everything to Allah, never to himself.

verses.ajuz: مَعَ ابۡنِ بِشۡرٍ ضَوۡؤُهُ فِي الۡحَالِكَةۡ
verses.tr: ʿImrān was greeted by the angels, while Ibn Bishr was granted a light that shone through the darkness.

exp.en:
Two further accounts are mentioned here: the greeting of the angels to ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn رضي الله عنه and the light that appeared for ʿAbbād ibn Bishr رضي الله عنه and his companion.

1. The angels greeting ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn

ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn رضي الله عنه was a noble Companion. The angels would greet him, shake his hand and, according to the reports, he would hear them speaking.

Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Ḥajar mentions in Fatḥ al-Bārī that it is authentically established that ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn رضي الله عنه used to hear the speech of the angels.

Another report, narrated by al-Ṭabarānī in al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr, states that the angels would shake his hand until he underwent cauterisation.

The report explains that ʿImrān رضي الله عنه suffered from haemorrhoids and used cauterisation as a treatment. According to this narration, the angels stopped greeting him after he underwent the treatment. However, this particular report has been weakened by a number of ḥadīth scholars, who considered it objectionable. Allah knows best.

2. The light of ʿAbbād ibn Bishr and his companion

The second account concerns ʿAbbād ibn Bishr رضي الله عنه and his companion Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr رضي الله عنه.

One night, the two Companions left the company of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It was extremely dark, but a light appeared before them, resembling the tip of a whip. It illuminated the path ahead, allowing them to see where they were walking.

When they eventually separated, the light divided with them, and each one had his own light to guide him along his way.

Anas رضي الله عنه narrates:

“Two men left the Prophet ﷺ on a dark night, and a light appeared before them. When they separated, the light separated with them.”

The narrations identify these two Companions as Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr and ʿAbbād ibn Bishr رضي الله عنهما.

These accounts illustrate two further forms of karāmah: the extraordinary experience of hearing and being greeted by the angels, and the appearance of light that illuminated the way through the darkness.

Translator’s reflection

The symbolism of light is profound. The Qurʾān repeatedly links faith with light. Allah says: ﴿اللَّهُ وَلِيُّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا يُخْرِجُهُمْ مِنَ الظُّلُمَاتِ إِلَى النُّورِ﴾ “Allah is the Protector of those who believe. He brings them out of darkness into light.” (al-Baqarah 2:257) For these Companions, Allah manifested that reality physically. Their outward light reflected the inward light already filling their hearts.

Living this bayt

Most believers will never witness angels greeting them. Nor will a light appear before them in the darkness. Yet every believer who follows the Qurʾān and Sunnah walks with a greater light: The light of guidance.

That light accompanies him not merely through the darkness of night, but through the darkness of life itself.

verses.tr: How many supplications of the noble Companions were answered! Among them were Saʿīd and Saʿd, those courageous men of great resolve.

exp.en:
The answered supplications of the noble Companions رضي الله عنهم provide further examples of karāmāt. Two such examples are the supplications of Saʿīd ibn Zayd and Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ رضي الله عنهما, both of whom were among the ten Companions promised Paradise.

1. The supplication of Saʿīd ibn Zayd

Saʿīd ibn Zayd رضي الله عنه was one of the ten companions promised Paradise. A woman named Arwā bint al-Ḥakam once accused him of taking part of her land and changing the boundary markers between their properties.

She took the matter to Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam. Saʿīd رضي الله عنه denied the accusation and said that he would never take even a portion of her land after hearing the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: “Whoever wrongfully takes even a handspan of land will have it placed around his neck down to the seven earths.”

Marwān then told him that no further evidence was needed after hearing this.

Saʿīd رضي الله عنه supplicated: “O Allah, if she is lying, then take away her sight and cause her to die on her own land.”

Allah accepted his duʿā’; she eventually lost her eyesight. Later, while walking on her land, she fell into a pit and died.

This was one of the clear karāmāt granted to Saʿīd ibn Zayd through the acceptance of his sincere supplication.

2. The supplication of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ

Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ رضي الله عنه was also one of the ten companions promised Paradise, and his supplications were known to be answered.

While serving as governor of Kūfah, a man falsely accused him before ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رضي الله عنه, claiming that he did not lead military expeditions properly, distribute wealth fairly, or judge justly. He even accused him of not performing his ṣalāh correctly.

When Saʿd رضي الله عنه heard these accusations, he reminded them of his standing among the earliest Muslims: “I was the seventh among seven with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he once said to me, ‘Shoot, O Saʿd!’ May my father and mother be sacrificed for you.’ Now the people of Banū Asad criticize me regarding my Islam?”

Saʿd رضي الله عنه supplicated against the man: “O Allah! If this servant of Yours is lying, has stood only for showing off, and has made this accusation falsely, then prolong his life, prolong his poverty, and expose him to trials.”

Allah answered his duʿā’. The man lived to an extremely old age, until his eyebrows drooped over his eyes. He became extremely poor and would ask people for assistance. He would also follow young women through the streets. When people asked him about his condition, he would say: “I am an old man afflicted by trials. The supplication of Saʿd has befallen me.”

These two accounts illustrate the answered supplications of Saʿīd ibn Zayd and Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ رضي الله عنهما, further demonstrating the karāmāt Allah granted to His righteous servants.

The phrase “ذلك الليث الهمام“ (“that courageous lion”) is simply a poetic expression describing Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ (رضي الله عنه) as a brave and valiant warrior, included to complete the metre of the poem.

Translator’s reflection

One lesson stands out. This teaches us that the greatest honour is not extraordinary ability, but extraordinary closeness to Allah. When the heart is sincere, the tongue is truthful, and one’s livelihood is pure, Allah opens doors that no worldly means can explain.

Living this bayt

Every believer should aspire to become someone whose duʿāʾ carries weight before Allah. How?

By purifying one’s heart, earning lawfully, obeying Allah in private and public, and following the Sunnah. The goal is not to be known as someone whose prayers are answered. The goal is to become someone whom Allah loves.

The acceptance of duʿāʾ is one of the beautiful consequences of that relationship.

sadrW.g: Safīnah (freed slave of the Prophet ﷺ)

ajuzW.g: so they set their backs (to the mountain)

verses.tr: Safīnah walked on while a lion followed behind him, and ʿUmar called out, “O Sāriyah!” and they took their position against it.

exp.en:
Two further accounts of extraordinary occurrences involving the Companions رضي الله عنهم are mentioned here: the incident of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رضي الله عنه calling out to Sāriyah during battle, and the incident of Safīnah رضي الله عنه encountering a lion.

1. Safīnah and the lion

Safīnah رضي الله عنه was a noble Companion and the freed servant of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

On one occasion, while travelling along a road, a lion appeared before him. Safīnah رضي الله عنه addressed the lion, informing it that he was the Messenger of Allah’s ﷺ Messenger.

The lion then lowered its head and began walking alongside him, accompanying and protecting him along the road until he reached his destination.

2. ʿUmar’s call to Sāriyah

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رضي الله عنه once sent a Muslim army to Persia and appointed a man named Sāriyah as its commander.

While ʿUmar رضي الله عنه was delivering a sermon from the pulpit in Madīnah, he suddenly began calling out:

يَا سَارِيَةُ الْجَبَلَ! يَا سَارِيَةُ الْجَبَلَ! يَا سَارِيَةُ الْجَبَلَ!

“O Sāriyah! The mountain! O Sāriyah! The mountain!”

He was instructing Sāriyah to position his army by the mountain and take shelter with it at their backs.

Sometime later, a messenger from the army arrived. ʿUmar رضي الله عنه asked him what had happened. He explained that the Muslims had encountered the enemy and were being defeated when they suddenly heard a voice calling: يَا سَارِيَةُ الْجَبَلَ

They immediately positioned themselves with their backs against the mountain, and Allah granted them victory over the enemy.

These two incidents provide further examples of extraordinary occurrences granted to the Companions: the remarkable call of ʿUmar رضي الله عنه that reached an army far away, and the lion that accompanied Safīnah رضي الله عنه on his journey.

Translator’s reflection

One of the most beautiful lessons here is that Allah’s creation is entirely under His command. The lion obeys Him. zDistance obeys Him. Sound obeys Him. Mountains obey Him. Time and space are servants of their Creator. If He wills that a lion becomes a guide rather than a predator, it does. If He wills that a voice cross hundreds of miles, it does. The extraordinary is effortless for the One Who created the ordinary.

Living this bayt

The believer places his trust not in worldly causes but in the Lord of those causes. We make use of the means available to us, but our confidence rests in Allah alone. When He wills to protect His servant, He may do so through ordinary means or through means that leave people astonished. Either way, the Protector is always the same.

verses.tr: The fire did not burn Ibn Thuwab, and the sea did not drown Ibn al-Ḥaḍramī.

exp.en:
Two remarkable accounts are mentioned here: the protection of Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī from fire, and the extraordinary events associated with al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Ḥaḍramī رضي الله عنه when crossing water.

1. Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī and the fire

Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī رحمه الله, whose name was ʿAbdullāh ibn Thuwab, was a distinguished Tābiʿī. When al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī falsely claimed Prophethood, he summoned Abū Muslim and asked him: “Do you testify that I am the Messenger of Allah?”

Abū Muslim replied: “I cannot hear what you are saying.”

Al-Aswad then asked: “Do you testify that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah?”

He replied: “Yes.”

Al-Aswad ordered that a fire be prepared and Abū Muslim be thrown into it. However, when they looked, they found him standing inside the fire, performing ṣalāh. Allah had made the fire cool and safe for him, just as He had done for Ibrāhīm عليه السلام.

After the death of the Prophet ﷺ, Abū Muslim travelled to Madīnah. When ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb رضي الله عنه met him, he seated him between himself and Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq رضي الله عنهما, saying: “Praise be to Allah, Who did not cause me to die until I saw someone from the nation of Muḥammad to whom the same was done as was done to Ibrāhīm, the close friend of Allah.”

2. Al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Ḥaḍramī and the crossing of water

Al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Ḥaḍramī رضي الله عنه was a noble Companion who was appointed by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as his governor in Bahrain. His supplications were known to be answered.

His frequent duʿā’ was:

يَا عَلِيْمُ يَا حَليْمُ يَا عَلِيُّ يَا عَظِيْمُ

“O All-Knowing, O Forbearing, O Most High, O Most Great.”

When he and his companions once ran out of water, he supplicated to Allah for rain so that they could drink and perform wuḍūʾ. Allah answered his supplication, and water came down for them.

On another occasion, while leading an army towards Persia, they encountered the sea and could not cross it with their horses. ʿAlāʾ رضي الله عنه supplicated to Allah and then instructed the army: “Proceed with the help of Allah.”

The entire army crossed over the water to the other side, and the saddles of their horses did not even become wet.

Abū Hurayrah رضي الله عنه was among the soldiers who witnessed this incident and narrated it. He also supplicated to Allah that his body should not be seen when he died. When he eventually passed away, his body could not be found in the grave.

3. Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī crossing the river

A similar incident is also reported concerning Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī رحمه الله, the same Tābiʿī who was thrown into the fire.

On one occasion, he and the soldiers accompanying him crossed the River Tigris on foot, even though the water was extremely high, carrying large pieces of timber. He instructed the army to walk across the water. He then turned to his companions and asked whether any of them had lost any belongings, so that he could supplicate to Allah for them.

One man said that he had lost his mikhlāh (مِخْلَاة), a small bag. Abū Muslim told him to follow, and they found the bag caught on something in the water. He retrieved it for him.

It is also reported that a woman once placed poison in Abū Muslim’s food, but it did not harm him.

These accounts illustrate the extraordinary protection and assistance Allah granted to these righteous servants, demonstrating His support for those who sincerely believe, obey Him, and follow His Messenger ﷺ.

Translator’s reflection

One of the greatest mistakes people make is to imagine that nature possesses autonomous power. The Qurʾān teaches otherwise. Fire does not burn because it has independent authority. Water does not drown because it possesses inherent sovereignty. Both operate according to laws created by Allah. When He wishes, those laws continue. When He wishes, they are suspended. This strengthens tawḥīd. It shifts our reliance away from created means and towards the Creator of those means.

Living this bayt

Every believer relies on ordinary means. We seek warmth from fire. We travel across water. We take medicine when ill. Islam never tells us to abandon the means. Rather, it teaches us never to place our ultimate trust in them.

The means are created. Allah alone is the Creator.

verses.tr: The dirhams of ʿĀmir increased, and the horse of Ṣilah was brought back to life.

exp.en:
The following accounts concern two distinguished Tābiʿīn, ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Qays and Ṣilah ibn Ashyam رحمهما الله, who were granted several extraordinary occurrences.

1. The dirhams of ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Qays

ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Qays رحمه الله was a distinguished Tābiʿī. He would receive an allowance of two thousand dirhams, which he kept in the sleeve of his garment. In those days, the sleeve commonly served as a place to keep one’s money.

Whenever he encountered someone in need along the road, he would give that person money without counting it. Yet, when he returned home, the number and weight of his dirhams remained unchanged.

On another occasion, he passed a caravan that had been blocked by a lion. He approached the lion, touched it with his garment and placed his foot on its neck, saying: “You are merely one of the dogs of the Most Merciful, and I would be ashamed to fear anything besides Him.” The caravan then passed safely, and the lion did not harm them.

Among his other reported karāmāt, he supplicated to Allah to make purification easier for him during winter, and water would be brought to him while it was steaming.

He also asked Allah to prevent Shayṭān from distracting his heart while he was performing ṣalāh, and Shayṭān was unable to do so.

2. The horse of Ṣilah ibn Ashyam

Ṣilah ibn Ashyam رحمه الله was also a Tābiʿī who experienced several karāmāt.

On one occasion, he was out on a military expedition when his horse died. He supplicated: “O Allah, do not allow any created being to have a favour over me.”

He then supplicated to Allah, and his horse came back to life. He continued fighting on it until the battle ended and returned home riding the same horse. When he arrived home, he called his son and said: “My son, take the saddle of the horse, for it is only on loan.”

As soon as the saddle was removed, the horse died once again.

Another incident occurred when Ṣilah رحمه الله, while travelling through al-Ahwāz, became extremely hungry. He supplicated to Allah for food, whereupon a basket of fresh dates, wrapped in a silk cloth, appeared behind him. He ate the dates, while the cloth remained with his wife for a long time.

On another occasion, while he was performing ṣalāh at night in a wooded area, a lion approached him. When he completed his ṣalāh, Ṣilah calmly addressed it, saying: “Seek your provision somewhere other than this place.”

The lion then turned away, roaring as it left.

These narrations illustrate how Allah honoured His righteous servants with extraordinary occurrences, not because they sought miracles, but because of their sincerity, complete trust in Allah, and steadfast obedience to Him.

Translator’s reflection

There is an important spiritual lesson hidden here. Allah did not increase the dirhams merely to make someone wealthy. Nor did He revive the horse merely to amaze people. Every karāmah in this poem serves a higher purpose. Strengthening faith. Facilitating obedience. Supporting the righteous. This is fundamentally different from the sensationalism that often surrounds discussions of miracles.

Living this bayt

We often ask Allah for more. More wealth. More strength. More opportunities. This bayt reminds us that what we should truly seek is barakah. A little with Allah’s blessing accomplishes far more than abundance without His blessing.

Likewise, every blessing He grants us - whether health, wealth, transport, or ability - is a means to draw nearer to Him, not an end in itself.

verses.ajuz: ذُو الۡعَرۡشِ مِنۡ دَلۡوٍ بِهِ رِوَاهَا
verses.tr: And Umm Ayman, whom the Lord of the Mighty Throne gave to drink, quenching her thirst from a bucket, granting her complete relief from thirst.

exp.en:
رِوَاهَا

رِوَاهَا is derived from الرِّيُّ, meaning the removal of thirst and the complete satisfaction of one’s need for water

Umm Ayman رضي الله عنها, whose name was Barakah al-Ḥabashiyyah, was a noble Companion and the caretaker of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ during his childhood.

During one of her migrations, she had no food or water with her. The journey became so difficult that she was close to dying from hunger and thirst. When the time came to break her fast, she heard a sound above her. Raising her head, she saw a bucket suspended above her. She drank from it until her thirst was completely quenched.

From that day onwards, she never experienced thirst again for the remainder of her life.

This was one of the extraordinary provisions Allah granted her, a clear example of a karāmah.

Translator’s reflection

Perhaps this is one of the most comforting examples in the poem. The Lord of the Mighty Throne noticed the thirst of one woman. If He cared for Umm Ayman’s thirst in the desert... How much more should the believer trust that Allah knows every hidden hardship he carries?

Our problems may appear small in the eyes of people.

They are never small in the sight of Allah.

Living this bayt

Every sip of water reminds us of this lesson. We often thank the person who handed us the glass. But beyond every visible hand is the Hand of Allah. He is الساقي in the ultimate sense. Every drop reaches us because He willed it.

The believer therefore lives in continual gratitude, recognising Allah’s care in both the extraordinary and the ordinary.

verses.tr: All praise belongs to Allah, who has honoured His righteous servants with karāmāt (miraculous favours) and bestowed these blessings upon them.

exp.en:
The author concludes the poem by praising Allah for granting extraordinary gifts to His awliyā’, acknowledging that every karāmah is purely a favour and grace from Him, not something earned independently by the servant.

Translator’s reflection

There is a subtle lesson hidden in the structure of the poem. The author spends many verses describing extraordinary events. Yet he never says: “Praise be to the awliyāʾ.” He says: “Praise be to Allah.” That single shift protects the reader from one of the greatest dangers in this subject: Allowing admiration for the servant to eclipse admiration for the Creator.

The awliyāʾ point us to Allah. They never replace Him.

Living this bayt

When we hear about the lives of the righteous, our hearts should not become attached to extraordinary stories. They should become attached to the Lord who honoured those servants. If reading about the awliyāʾ increases our love for Allah, then we have understood the purpose of these narrations. If it merely amazes us, then we have missed the deeper lesson.

verses.tr: And al-Lālakāʾī has devoted extensive attention to this subject, narrating nearly two hundred accounts of the karāmāt of the awliyāʾ.

exp.en:
The author concludes by referring to Imām al-Lālakāʾī (رحمه الله), Hibatullāh ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Manṣūr al-Ṭabarī, one of the great scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah.

He authored the famous work Sharḥ Uṣūl Iʿtiqādi Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamāʿah, a multi-volume compilation on Islamic creed. The fifth volume is devoted almost entirely to the karāmāt of the awliyā’, in which he narrates, with authentic chains of transmission, more than two hundred reports concerning the miraculous events experienced by the Companions and the Tābiʿūn.

Many of the examples mentioned throughout this poem are drawn from the narrations preserved in his work. His book remains one of the most important classical references documenting the creed of Ahl al-Sunnah regarding the karāmāt of the righteous.

Translator’s reflection

One of the greatest lessons here concerns scholarship itself. The author does not say: “Believe these stories because I have mentioned them.” Instead, he says: “Return to the books of the scholars.”

This cultivates confidence in the tradition rather than dependence upon the individual author. It also teaches students an important principle: Our religion is built upon transmitted knowledge, carefully preserved generation after generation.

Living this bayt

There is a subtle invitation in this verse. Do not stop at summaries. Do not be content with quotations. Return to the original works of the scholars.

The more one studies the heritage of Ahl al-Sunnah, the more one appreciates the precision with which they preserved both creed and history.

verses.tr: And we ask Allah to grant us safety in our religion and our worldly lives, and to bless us with steadfastness.

exp.en:
The author concludes this forty-one-verse poem with a heartfelt supplication, asking Allah to grant us well-being and safety in both our religion and our worldly affairs. He prays that Allah makes him, and everyone who reads or studies this poem and its explanation, among those who remain steadfast upon the Straight Path until they meet Him.

He then ends with praise to Allah, acknowledging that every righteous achievement is completed only through His favour and grace:

الحمد لله الذي بنعمته تتم الصالحات

“All praise belongs to Allah, by whose blessing all righteous deeds are brought to completion.”

Translator’s reflection

There is something deeply moving here. Imagine reading an entire poem about miraculous events... and then the author concludes by asking only for steadfastness. That tells us everything. The awliyāʾ themselves never sought extraordinary experiences. They sought Allah. If Allah honoured them with karāmāt, they thanked Him. If He did not, they remained content. Their greatest concern was to die as believers. That is why Shaykh Waleed ends with istiqāmah.

Living this bayt

This should become the believer’s daily duʿāʾ. Not: “O Allah, grant me extraordinary experiences.” Rather: “O Allah, preserve my dīn. Protect my worldly affairs from leading me astray. Keep me steadfast until I meet You.” If Allah grants that, He has granted the greatest success.

Translator’s conclusion

If there is only one lesson we take away from this entire work, let it be the fourteenth bayt: “Know that the greatest of all miracles is to worship Allah with steadfastness.”

How often we marvel at the extraordinary: someone walking upon water, travelling great distances in an instant, or witnessing something beyond the customary order of things. Yet we sometimes overlook a far greater miracle: a servant who worships Allah consistently, remains sincere in his devotion, and holds firmly to the Qur’an and Sunnah until his final breath.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught us that the most beloved deeds to Allah are those performed consistently, even if they are small: أحب الأعمال إلى الله أدومها وإن قل.

This is where true greatness lies. Not necessarily in extraordinary displays, but in ordinary acts of worship performed with extraordinary perseverance.

We need not spend our lives searching for the ability to fly or walk upon water. And if we ever witness such occurrences, we must not be carried away by amazement. Rather, we should carefully examine the person’s adherence to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ. As the scholars reminded us, even if you see someone walking upon water, do not be deceived until you have measured his conduct against the Qur’an and Sunnah.

Ultimately, the greatest karāmah is not that Allah enables a person to do something extraordinary, but that He grants him the ability to remain obedient to Him. To preserve one’s prayers, guard one’s heart, uphold the rights of others, remain sincere, and continue upon the path of righteousness, day after day, until death.

We therefore conclude with the very supplication with which the author concludes his poem: that Allah grant us well-being in our religion and our worldly affairs and bless us with steadfastness.

May Allah grant us beneficial knowledge, sincere deeds, sound belief, and unwavering istiqāmah. May He protect our hearts from deviation, keep our feet firm upon the Straight Path, and allow us to meet Him while He is pleased with us.

For indeed, if Allah grants a servant istiqāmah until his final breath, He has granted him the greatest of all miracles.

وصلى الله وسلم وبارك على نبينا محمد، وعلى آله وصحبه أجمعين.

والحمد لله رب العالمين.

Abdullah Badat
